ABSTRACT: The excited-state proton transfer (ESPT) reaction is an
important primary photochemical process because it is closely related to
photophysical properties. Although ESPT research in aqueous solutions is
predominant, alcoholic solvent-mediated ESPT studies are also significant in
terms of photoacid−based reactions. Especially, the research for dihydrox-
ynaphthalenes (DHNs) has been largely neglected due to the challenging data
interpretation of two hydroxyl groups. A novel fluorescent dye, resveratrone,
synthesized by light irradiation of resveratrol, which is famous for its antioxidant
properties, can be regarded as a type of DHN, and it has distinctive optical
properties, including high quantum yield, a large two-photon absorption
coefficient, a large Stokes shift, and very high biocompatibility. In this study, we
investigate the overall kinetics of the optical properties of resveratrone and find
evidence for alcoholic solvent-mediated ESPT involvement in the radiative
properties of resveratrone with a large Stokes shift. Our investigation provides an opportunity to revisit the overlooked photophysical
properties of intriguing photoacid behavior and the large Stokes shift of the dihydroxynaphthalene dye.

INTRODUCTION
Excited-state proton transfer (ESPT) is an important primary
photochemical process that comprises a huge area in the
investigation of photophysics.
1−5
When the electron redis-
tribution in the excited state weakens the O−H or N−H bond,
the proton can migrate to a hydrogen acceptor group or an
adjacent solvent molecule. When the proton is transferred to
surrounding solvents, because this interaction is like an acid−
base relationship, such molecules are called photoacids and
commonly display emission with a large Stokes shift or
sometimes dual emission.
5−7
Although the phenomenon is
largely investigated in the aqueous environment, ESPT
dynamics in an alcoholic solvent is also an equally important
area, especially from the perspective of photoacid−based
catalysis, including O-glycosylation and dihydroxylation of
alcohols to hydrocarbons.
3,8,9
Therefore, in order to identify
the potential application of a photoacid, it is essential to
investigate the ESPT dynamics while considering the role of
the environment.
Resveratrone is a novel fluorophore synthesized by light
irradiation of resveratrol, which is a type of stilbenoid
commonly found in berries and famous for its antioxidant,
cardioprotective, and anticancerous properties.
10,11
The
precursor resveratrol is weakly emissive in both trans- and
cis-forms. The initial photoreaction of trans-resveratrol is
isomerization into cis-resveratrol, which remains dark, but
when it is irradiated further, this molecule gets converted into a
highly fluorescent compound, resveratrone (Figure. 1a).
12
In
addition to simple and straightforward synthesis, as it only
involves light irradiation and purification, resveratrone
possesses several useful properties as a fluorophore, including
high quantum yield, large Stokes shift and two-photon
absorption coefficient, and very high biocompatibility.
12,13
Despite its high potential application for biological discipline,
the study of its photophysical process is still lacking, and the
ground for its large Stokes shift and quantum yield remains
elusive. This lack hinders further utilization of the compound.
From a structural point of view, resveratrone can be
regarded as a derivative of 1,3-dihydroxynaphthalene (1,3-
DHN) with an additional functional group extending π-
conjugation. Such hydroxyl-functionalized groups attached to
aromatic rings like benzene and naphthalene are commonly
known to display the ESPT process, which may take time up to
nanoseconds.
1,2,14−16
Also, as a model compound, pH-
dependent absorption and emission change of naphthols are
well reported in several literature studies that include 1,3-
DHN.
3,17

Through quantum calculations and comparisons with naph-

EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
Synthesis of Resveratrone. A 125 μM methanol solution
(300 mL) of resveratrol (R5010, Sigma) was irradiated with
UV light for 4 min using four 6-W UV lamps (λ
max
= 305 nm)
at room temperature. Synthesized resveratrone was isolated
from the remaining precursor and side products using
preparatory thin-layer chromatography, where the mobile
phase was composed of methanol and methylene chloride
(1:20). The resulting compound was confirmed using
absorption and
1
H NMR spectra, which are in agreement
with previously reported values.
12
Photophysical Properties. Femtosecond transient ab-
sorption spectroscopy was conducted using a conventional
pump−probe setup under ambient conditions. The optical
source was a regeneratively amplified Ti:sapphire laser
(Spectra-Physics) with an average power of 0.65 μJ/pulse, a
pulse width of 130 fs fwhm, and a repetition rate of 1 kHz at an
800 nm output wavelength. Pump pulses of 400 nm were
generated using a second harmonic generator (TP1A, Spectra-
Physics), filtered down by a quartz neutral density filter, and
used at 1 mW. A continuum light, which was used as the probe
pulse, was generated by focusing the 800 nm light by using a
UV-fused silica plano convex lens (CVI Melles Griot, f = 100
mm) onto a sapphire plate (WG31050, Thorlabs). The time
delay between the pump and probe pulses was scanned using a
Daedal 404300XRMP delay stage (Parker). The pump pulses
were modulated by using an optical chopper (MC1000,
Thorlabs) synchronized to the laser. The probe pulses of the
signal were detected by photodiodes (2031, New Focus) after
wavelength selection using a monochromator (250 IS/SM,
Chromex, 600 grooves/mm grating blazed at 750 nm).
Transient absorption signals were obtained by using a lock-in
amplifier (SR830, Stanford Research Systems).
The fluorescence lifetimes of resveratrone were measured
with a time-correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC) board
(SPC-150, Becker &Hickl) with a 48.9 ps time channel. The
excitation source was a 405 nm picosecond-pulsed diode laser
(LDH−P-C-405, Picoquant). The decay lifetimes of different
wavelengths were acquired using various bandpass filters.
Quantum calculations were performed using the DFT and
TDDFT methods at the B3LYP/6-311G(d,p) level of theory
using the Gaussian09 package. Molecular structures and
orbitals were visualized with GaussView 5.0.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Figure 1b shows steady-state absorption and emission spectra
of resveratrone dissolved in methanol, which is clearly different
from its synthesis precursor, trans-resveratrol.
21
As expected
from its yellowish color, resveratrone displays a strong
absorption below 400 nm. The absorption extends to longer
wavelengths, although the absorbance is quite low (inset). This
is consistent with the previously reported values of the
compound. When irradiated, it emits photoluminescence
centered near 550 nm, showing a bright yellow-green color.
The apparent large Stokes shift is up to almost 150 nm, which
is the typical characteristic of the ESPT molecule.
22

Based on this, we can list the possible ions and the electronic

assignment of the species of resveratrone and its two possible
monoanionic forms is done using quantum calculations, the

Although the model is without the solvent cage, it can provide

The first thing to note is that the HOMO−LUMO gaps of
anionic forms are significantly smaller than that of molecular

To confirm the involvement of hydroxyl anions, we attempt
to observe the effect of the pH on the steady-state spectrum of
resveratrone. We conducted the acid−base analysis of an 80
μM resveratrone solution in 20 mL of water, subjected to
titration with a 22 mM NaOH solution. The pH change is
gradual (Figure S2), reflecting complex equilibrium conditions
between the solvent and different forms of resveratrone,
including molecular, monoionic, and di-ionic forms. Figure 3
illustrates the effect of NaOH addition on the absorption and
emission spectra of the resveratrone solution, providing
insights into the wavelengths absorbed by the compound.
These spectra change incrementally with each addition of 20
μL of the NaOH solution. Even a very small addition of NaOH
alters the absorption spectrum significantly. A rising peak
under highly basic conditions near 415 nm also appears in the
methanol spectrum as a small shoulder in the inset of Figure
1b. The observation in different buffer solutions indicates that
it is indeed the effect of pH (Figure S3). Here, the emission
profile stays almost consistent, but the fluorescence is
quenched as more NaOH is added. This behavior is
consistently recreated with resveratrone in methanol when a
NaOH solution is added (Figure S4).
This trend can be explained by adopting the solvation
model. However, just a simple solvatochromic trend and the
presence of two different anions can no longer explain the
photoluminescence behavior of resveratrone in alcoholic
solvents, but they are shown to be in a more intimate
relationship. Therefore, we adopt a two-step Eigen−Weller
model where the proton-transferred solvent forms intermediate
contact ion pairs (CIPs) with the photoacid molecule.
24,25
In
alcoholic solvents, naphthols are known to form hydrogen-
bonded clusters with surrounding solvent molecules.
3
Because
they are in close contact, the proton-accepting ability and
relaxation of the solvents deeply influence the kinetics of
photoacids, especially the formation and dissociation of CIPs.
Indeed, the quantum yield of resveratrone is also known to
be highly dependent on the type of solvent used.

In order to directly track the real-time dynamics of the
fluorescence, the transient absorption of resveratrone using a
400 nm pump (1 mW) has been measured. Figure 4a,b shows
the resulting spectrum in the visible range, using probe
wavelengths from 470 to 720 nm. From the energy shift, the
evolution between multiple excited states is obvious from the
transient absorption spectra. The signals appear and disappear
in distinctively different time scales, and it can be clearly seen
in the selected time profiles presented in Figure 4c. The rise
and fall distinguish two lifetime components in the picosecond
dynamics of resveratrone, where the lifetime of the first
component is 6.4 ps and that of the second component is
120.6 ps (for fitting, see Figure S8).
Briefly, the initial excited state is shown at 0.5 ps with a 500
nm SE peak that undergoes a significant wavelength shift,
which can be considered as the basis for the large Stokes shift
of resveratrone. Such a large energy shift is typical of ESPT,
but the assignation of each transition is challenging and
requires a careful look.
22
With time, the stimulated emission
(SE) peak shifts toward the longer wavelength region,
indicating the transition to the energetically relaxed state.
Indeed, at 1 ps, the spectrum shows a markedly red-shifted
peak and a stronger SE signal, where at this point, it could be
considered as emission observed in the steady state, mainly
contributed by the ionic state. Since the absorption edge is
considered to be below 450 nm, the proton dissociation
process can be regarded as having been completed within the
subpicosecond scale.
The mechanism behind this can be explained by the fact that
the molecule and the solvent already form an intimate
interaction via hydrogen bonding and instantly form the CIP
in the excited state. This allows the proton transfer to proceed
without structural alteration. As time passes, the spectrum
evolves into another form, which has strong excited-state
absorption (ESA) below 500 nm and SE peaks near 550 nm.
The decay of the excited-state absorption signal at 680 nm
occurs in a time scale similar to the rise of ESA at 490 nm.
However, intriguingly, the SE peak keeps shifting almost up to
600 nm, whereafter it decays monoexponentially without
spectral change, suggesting the involvement of more than two
fluorescent species in the dynamics.
Linking the experimental lifetimes with specific excited-state
molecular species is not an easy task, especially since
resveratrone does not have any previous in-depth study of
photophysical properties. We turn to an analogous study for
identifying species instead. The report of analogous compound
1,3-DHN reports complex multiexponential kinetics that
heavily depend on pH.
29
Similar to the case of resveratrone,
1,3-DHN is suspected to have different excited species.
However, their emission maxima at high pH overlap
significantly, so it is very challenging to distinguish. The
different excited-state species had two distinctive lifetimes and
could be resolved. They are explained by the different anions
generated by deprotonation of the hydroxyl group at the 1- and
3-site of naphthalene. In another case, Agbaria et al.
encountered an unusual peak shift problem during titration
of 1,6-dihydroxynaphthalene and tentatively assigned the blue-
shifted emission of the compound as originating from the
dianions.
30
However, in our case, we can disregard this
possibility because the quantum calculation prediction of the
di-ionic form predicts an energy of 700 nm (Figure 2d), which
deviates significantly from the 580 nm peak we could observe
at the 50.7 ps transient spectrum. Indeed, the peak shift shown
in SE peaks is too small to be attributed to an additional
proton loss.
Following the methods, we also conducted fluorescence
lifetime measurements at different wavelengths by time-
correlated single-photon counting (TCSPC) in order to
distinguish different fluorescent species (Figure 4d−f). The
wavelength-dependent lifetimes are normalized and plotted
against wavelength to display different components participat-
ing in the fluorescence. The fluorescence lifetimes of
resveratrone in different alcohols are shown to appear in
time scales of few nanoseconds. The decay shows biexponen-
tial trends in all solvents, although in t-butanol, the longer
lifetime dominates to the point of almost monoexponential. In
methanol, the decay is almost consistent across emission
wavelengths. Here, the shorter component decays with lifetime
on a scale comparable to the longer ESA component of the TA
spectrum. The difference may originate from the large
instrument response function of the setup, which is
comparable to the longer decay lifetime of the transient
absorption signals and would not distinguish the shorter
lifetime kinetics. In ethanol and t-butanol, the lifetime of the
red-shifted wavelength region gets longer. The longer lifetime
after 500 nm could be attributed to fully relaxed resveratrone
species. Interestingly, the rise of photoluminescence after 500
nm matches 460 nm decay in t-butanol, suggesting a shift from
the higher to lower excited state, like kinetics observed in the
transient absorption of resveratrone in methanol, albeit in a
different time scale. The trend seems to be also related to the
quantum yield of resveratrone; the values in different alcoholic
solvents are presented in Table 2. Compared to other solvents,
resveratrone in methanol displays a significantly lower
quantum yield of 0.03. When the solvent is changed to t-
butanol, the quantum yield significantly increases to 0.43.
Using time-resolved methods, we have observed that in the
fluorescence kinetics of resveratrone, two or more energy levels
are involved, and their behavior is highly solvent-dependent.
Under strong basic conditions, as revealed by the titration
results, the compound becomes weakly fluorescent, meaning
that the initial 6.4 ps pathway is blocked, and the system
remains in the initial subpicosecond state. This can be
understood by recognizing the presence of two monoions
that are not directly interchangeable.
This insight, combined with the high solvent-dependent
quantum yield, can explain the role of the solvent in the
observed behavior. The role of protons is crucial here, as the
solvent’s nature affects how protons are exchanged between
the two hydroxyl functional groups at the 1- and 3-site. In the
ground state, these groups form an equilibrium, but in the

CONCLUSIONS
Excited-state dynamics of the novel biocompatible dye
resveratrone was extensively studied using various spectro-
scopic techniques. Through our investigation of the photo-
induced ESPT dynamics of the bifunctional photoacid
resveratrone in alcoholic media, we discovered the physical
basis behind its photoluminescence. One of the key factors was
the critical role of solvents in the excited-state dynamics of
resveratrone. In particular, under basic conditions, blocking the
ESPT pathway between different monoionic species results in
a weak fluorescence from the initial subpicosecond state. This
behavior occurs due to the fact that two monoionic forms are
not directly interchangeable. Such a dual-functionalized moiety
poses inherent challenges, resulting in only a partial picture
being drawn in this study. Yet, despite these complexities, we
can draw a conclusion from experimental evidence that the
hydrogen dynamics of resveratrone occurs in the excited state,
and it determines the overall quantum yield of the compound.

In summary, in contrast to typical MAPbI
3
polycrystalline
films, an exceptionally strong band-filling effect was observed
in FA
0.5
MA
0.5
Pb
0.5
Sn
0.5
I
3
polycrystalline films at mild light
concentration levels usable for practical CPVs. Inspired by this,
we proposed mixed Pb-Sn perovskite-based EBA-CPVs,
formed by inserting a thin ICBA layer as an electronic
barrier-inducing layer, where the electronic barrier between the
perovskite and the ICBA could be modulated by the strong
band-filling effect of perovskites. Mixed Pb-Sn perovskite-based
CPVs were fabricated to demonstrate proof-of-concept of
EBA-CPVs and systematically characterized to evaluate the
impact of the band-filling on the device performance of mixed
Pb-Sn perovskites. Under high excitation intensities, the ICBA-
introduced EBA-CPVs showed novel phenomena that were
not observed in conventional devices. Such results originated
from the dynamic modulation of the electronic barrier between
the perovskite and the ICBA layer by the band-filling effect of
the perovskite under concentrated illumination. Our results
report the first experimental demonstration of the fact that
when the barrier-inducing band alignment, which is considered
undesirable in a typical PV system, is combined with the
unique photophysical property of the photoactive layer, it can
boost the performance of a CPV system. We believe that the
implementation of highly efficient CPVs is feasible using mixed
Pb-Sn perovskite polycrystalline films. Our findings provide a
step forward in the development of advanced perovskite-based
PV systems that exceed the S-Q limit.

ABSTRACT: Iridium(III) organometallic complexes have been a key
component in commercialization of organic light-emitting diodes, but the direct
relationship between their structural features and photophysical properties has
not yet been fully established. Here, combined experimental and theoretical
studies are carried out to elucidate the main factors governing the quantum
efficiency of red phosphorescent emitters by using two heteroleptic iridium(III)
complexes with high geometrical similarity. It is found that two red-emitting
heteroleptic iridium complexes differing only in the steric direction of
phenylquinoline (pq) and phenylisoquinoline (piq) ligands, annotated Red-pq
and Red-piq, show clearly different degrees of distortion of the ligand geometry
in the excited state, which leads to the higher quantum yield of Red-piq than that
of Red-pq. This larger distortion of the piq ligand causes more suppressed
nonradiative decay of Red-piq than that of Red-pq which is the important factor
governing the higher quantum yield of Red-piq.
■
INTRODUCTION
Among the known phosphorescent emitters, iridium(III)
organometallic complexes have been widely utilized due to
their chemical inertness and good photo- and thermal
stability.
1−3
Due to the strong electron spin−orbit coupling
of the heavy metal center, the iridium(III) metal center
induces sufficient spin−orbit coupling to facilitate the
intersystem crossing (ISC) between the singlet and triplet
states, which is normally forbidden by the selection rule. This
allows for highly efficient phosphorescence emission at room
temperature,
4,5
as well as enabling nearly 100% internal
quantum efficiency by utilizing both singlet and triplet
excitons. Consequently, research and application interest
mainly lies in the development of organic light-emitting diodes
(OLEDs), making the study of factors affecting their quantum
yields crucial.
1,6,7
Most of the iridium(III) complexes developed over the past
two decades are homoleptic Ir(C^N)
3
and heteroleptic
Ir(C^N)
2
(L^X) complexes (C^N = cyclometalating main
ligand and L^X = ancillary ligand).
8,9
In particular, heteroleptic
bis-cyclometalated Ir(III) complexes have been the focus of
intensive research due to their easy preparation, high stability,
and facile color tunability compared to homoleptic analogues.
4
The typical form of heteroleptic bis-cyclometalated Ir(III)
complexes has phenyl−pyridine (ppy) derivatives as the main
ligand and acetyl-acetonate (acac) derivatives as the ancillary
ligand. In these complexes, the main ligand plays a key role in
determining the emission wavelength and dipole moment. By
tuning the π-system of the main ligand, it is possible to adjust
the emission wavelength from blue to red.
1,10,11
Although the
relationship between the methylation site on the cyclo-
metalating ligands and the orientation of their transition
dipole moment has been reported, the influence of the π-
system on photophysical properties has not been fully
elucidated.
12
Phenylquinoline (pq) and phenylisoquinoline (piq) are
among the most popular choices for main ligands in the
heteroleptic Ir(C^NN)
2
(acac) complexes for inducing red-
emitting phosphorescence.
13−15
They are structurally isomeric
to each other and differ only slightly in the orientation of the
quinoline and isoquinoline rings. The incorporation of
dimethylated pq and piq ligands in iridium complexes, denoted
Red-pq and Red-piq, results in noticeable but not very
apparent changes in steady-state properties (Figure 1).
In this study, using such iridium complexes with little
geometry difference, we present experimental and theoretical

METHODS
Sample Preparation. 7.6 mg of iridium-[2-(3,5-
dimethylphenyl)quinoline]2-acac (Red-pq) and iridium-[1-
(3,5-dimethylphenyl)isoquinoline]2-acac (Red-piq) was dis-
solved in 20 mL of five different organic solvents (acetonitrile,
acetone, tetrahydrofuran, toluene, and cyclohexane) to form
stock solutions. They were diluted for further use in steady-
state and time-resolved experiments.
Time-Resolved Fluorescence Measurement. TCSPC
measurements were conducted using FluoTime300 (Pico-
Quant), with an excitation wavelength of 510.5 nm and an
excitation bandpass filter of 4.8 nm. The detection wavelength
was fixed at 625.5 nm for both Red-pq and Red-piq, with a 27
nm bandpass filter, and the time bin of the measurement was
50 ps for short measurements and 2.5 ns for longer
measurements.
Transient Absorption Spectroscopy. A femtosecond
pulse (130 fs, 120 cm
−1
, 450 μJ/pulse, 1 kHz) centered at 800
nm was generated by a standard regenerative-amplified
Ti:sapphire laser (Hurricane, Spectra Physics). Continuum
light, which was used as the probe pulse, was generated by
focusing 800 nm light using a planoconvex lens ( f = 100) into
a sapphire plate (WG31050, Thorlabs). The pump pulses were
generated using a second harmonic generator (TP1A, Spectra
Physics), and their polarizations were oriented at a magic angle
with respect to probe pulses using a half-wave plate. The
optical time delay between the pump pulse and the continuum
pulse was adjusted using a delay stage (Daedal 404300XRMP,
Parker). The pump pulses were modulated using a
synchronized optical chopper (MC1000, Thorlabs). The
probe pulses of the signal were detected by photodiodes
(2031, New Focus) after wavelength selection using a
monochromator (model 250 is/sm, grating of 600 grooves
blazed at 730 nm, Chromex). The transient absorption signals
were obtained using a lock-in amplifier (SR830, SRS).
Steady-State Spectroscopy. UV/vis absorption spectra
and photoluminescence (PL) spectra were recorded using
Lambda 25 (PerkinElmer) and QM-3/2004SE (PTI),
respectively. Measurements were done under ambient
conditions.

22
and
LANL2DZ for the Ir metal center.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Powdered forms of the iridium complexes were dissolved in
aprotic solvents with different polarities (cyclohexane, toluene,
acetone, and acetonitrile, in the order of increasing polarity).
All measurements are done under ambient conditions,
reflecting the commonly experienced conditions. The two
iridium(III) complexes show highly similar absorption and PL
spectral profiles as shown in Figure 1a,b. In general, spectral
features of Red-piq appear to be red-shifted with respect to
those of Red-pq, reflecting a smaller energy gap of Red-piq and
the deeper red emission. The transitions that contribute to the
absorption bands could be roughly assigned based on their
relative oscillator strengths and transition energies.
6,28
The
singlet ligand-centered (LC) excited states appear below 400
nm, and the sharp features displayed above 400 nm originate
from singlet metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) states.
The featureless and weak absorption near 600 nm is from a
direct transition to triplet MLCT states due to the high spin−
orbit coupling capacity of the iridium metal.
The emissive state of iridium complexes is known to be
associated with the triplet MLCT state, possessing inherent
electrical polarization. The emission profile was consistent
regardless of the excitation wavelength (Figure S1), affirming
that the emission originates from the lowest excited state of the
given multiplicity. In all cases, they display a main peak emitted
from the triplet MLCT, and a side peak or shoulder on the
longer wavelengths, sometimes called vibrational satellites. The
apparent full width at half-maximum change is observed only

This trend is more detailed in Figure 2a, where we can see

The excited-state features of Red-pq and Red-piq turn out to
be quite distinct from each other (Figure 3), which is quite
intriguing, especially considering their similarities in the
steady-state spectra. As shown in Figure 1, the absorption
spectra of the two species exhibit a high degree of similarity,
indicating similar energy structures at the Franck−Condon
state. However, significant differences are observed in the
spectra in the excited state. Red-pq shows a rather uniform and
featureless ESA, except for troughs that correspond to the
ground-state bleaching and stimulated emission, whereas Red-
piq displays a prominent excited absorption peak near the
probe range of 600−650 nm. In acetone, the environment with
high polarity, no noticeable signal for ground-state bleaching
and the stimulated emission was detected despite the fact that
the probe wavelength covers the absorption and the emission
range. This reflects that the triplet excited state is better
coupled with the singlet ground state under nonpolar
conditions, and the transition efficiency is low under nonpolar
conditions.
The strong ESA peak of Red-piq, unseen in Red-pq, is
indicative of varying energy structures and transition dipole
moments in their excited states. This implies that the triplet
states of Red-pq and Red-piq have distinct electron
distributions and optimized geometries. Additionally, in film
forms, both compounds show a lack of transient features and a
very little difference in nonradiative decay rate (Figure S3 and
Table S2). Considering the geometrically restricted condition
imposed in the film condition, ESA likely arises from
conformational changes and is closely related to the higher
nonradiative decay rate of Red-piq in solution.
Our experimental results indicate that the phosphorescent
emitting states of two iridium(III) complexes are significantly
different electrically polarized states, where Red-pq is more
prone to the nonradiative decay process. To account for the
difference in the quantum yield between Red-pq and Red-piq,
theoretical analysis using CAM-B3LYP DFT calculations,
known to describe charge-separated excited states effectively,
were employed to gain deeper understanding.

CONCLUSIONS
In conclusion, we have found that in the triplet excited states,
ligand distortion occurs from electron movement toward one
ligand. Higher distortion restricts vibronic coupling with the
ground-state geometry, leading to suppressed nonradiative
decay and a higher quantum yield. The Red-piq compared to
Red-pq shows higher distortion. Our research interconnects
the intricate relationship between ligand geometry and
nonradiative decay dynamics in heteroleptic iridium(III)
complexes. The extent of distortion and its effect on the ISC
rate have been reported in tetrahedral complexes, for which it
is simpler to control the structural parameters with the dihedral
angle.
43

By employing two synchronized mode-locked femtosecond lasers and inter-
ferometric detection of the pump-probe spectra—referred to asasynchronous
and interferometric transient absorption—we have developed a method for
broad dynamic range and rapid data acquisition. Using asynchronous and
interferometric transient absorption, we examined photochemical changes
during femtosecond pump-probe experiments on all-inorganic cesium lead
halide nanomaterials. The laser pulse train facilitates photoreactions while
allowing real-time observation of charge carrier dynamics. In perovskite
nanocrystals undergoing photo-substitution of halide anions, transient
absorption spectra showed increasing bandgap energy and faster relaxation
dynamics as the Cl/Br ratio increased. For colloidal perovskite nanoplatelets,
continuous observation revealed both spectral and kinetic changes during the
light-induced coalescence of nanoplatelets, by analyzing temporal segments.
This integrated technique not only deepens understanding of exciton
dynamics and environmental inﬂuences in perovskite nanomaterials but also
establishes asynchronous and interferometric transient absorption as a
transformative tool for real-time observation of photochemical dynamics.
In spectroscopy, researchers frequently encounter a dilemma when
the tool they employ for observation—light—also triggers alterations in
their target materials and molecular systems. This problem is parti-
cularly pronounced for ultrafast spectroscopy methods. Here, pro-
longed exposure to high-energy laser light is imperative to capture
subtle and weak nonlinear responses. The situation underscores the
challenge: the acquisition of data under such circumstances becomes
demanding and, at times, seemingly impossible. Therefore, the
reduction of data acquisition (DAQ) time is essential when the
observed materials deviate from established photostability standards.
The efﬁcacy of asynchronous optical sampling in curtailing DAQ
time is well-established, as it eliminates the need for linear stages to
generate time delays between pump and probe pulses
1,2. Although
initially proposed and demonstrated nearly half a century ago, our
group has been in pursuit of advancing this technique across various
bandwidth ranges and has applied it to a wide array of biological and
material systems3–6. However, the broader research community in
ultrafast spectroscopy remains incompletely cognizant of its utility for
rapid and stable transient absorption and multidimensional spectro-
scopic measurements. In this work, we introduce and apply our novel
spectroscopic approach, asynchronous and interferometric transient
absorption (AI-TA)
7, to investigate the photochemical reactions of
perovskite nanocrystals (PeNCs) and nanoplatelets (PeNPLs).
Perovskite nanomaterials have attracted considerable attention
for their applications, such as light-emitting diodes8 and single-photon
sources in quantum technologies9. Despite their susceptibility to form

Given their potential applications in solar cells and light-emitting
devices, the interaction of perovskites with light has become a subject
of signiﬁcant interest among researchers and engineers. Beyond time-
resolved studies of carrier and quasiparticle dynamics, perovskite
nanomaterials display a range of light-induced behaviors, including
degradation, which has emerged as a key focus in recent research.
Here, utilizing the rapid DAQ capabilities of AI-TA, we simultaneously
investigate both ultrafast carrier dynamics via femtosecond pump-

nanomaterials, where two distinct types of photoreactions are

The ﬁrst study examines photoinduced halide substitution of
PeNCs. A key feature of PeNCs is their possibility of post-synthesis
compositional modiﬁcation through the use of appropriate salts con-
taining halide anions, as they can freely diffuse into and out of the rigid
cation lattice
18. The halide composition signi ﬁcantly in ﬂuences the
bandgap energy, allowing the emission wavelength to be tuned across
the visible spectrum. For instance, iodide-based PeNCs exhibit red to
near-infrared emission, while bromide and chloride shift the bandgap
toward blue and near-ultraviolet regions
13.
Recent studies have reported halide anion substitution in per-
ovskites through a photoinduced process19,20. This phenomenon can
take place when PeNCs are dissolved in halide-containing solvents
(e.g., chloroform and dibromomethane) and concomitantly exposed
to light. The proposed mechanism involves the dissociation of solvent
molecules upon interaction with photoexcited PeNCs, facilitated by
interfacial electron transfer
19,21. The high reduction potential of these
solvents relative to PeNCs enables photoinduced electron transfer,
extracting halide anions from the solvents. These anions can then
exchange and diffuse within the PeNC lattice. The photoinduced
anion-exchange process allows remote control over the extent and
composition of substitution
20 while preserving the size and morphol-
ogy of the nanoparticles22. Additionally, it has been shown to mitigate
vacancy defects, enhance crystallinity23, and facilitate cation exchan-

The second system under investigation involves photon-driven
transformations of PeNPLs. PeNPLs represent a distinct class of
nanomaterials with unique morphology and physical properties com-
pared to PeNCs. Their deﬁning characteristic arises from conﬁnement
along a single-dimensional axis, with thinner platelets exhibiting
higher bandgap energy
25. However, their colloidal stability in solution
is limited, and PeNPLs are known to aggregate into higher-order
structures, including bulk-like status when exposed to heat 26,27,
light28–31, polar solvents32, or prolonged ambient conditions33. Particu-
larly, this phenomenon occurring under light exposure is referred to as
photon-driven transformation.
Such behavior is not exclusive to PeNPLs and can also occur in
other colloidal forms, including PeNCs and perovskite nanorods
34.
However, PeNPLs are especially prone to aggregation into higher-

into self-assembled superlattices, where discrete nanoplatelets stack
with ligands spacing the ionic crystal layers

assemblies may aggregate into larger structures, sometimes forming

In this Communication, we begin by providing an overview of our
approach, AI-TA, emphasizing how its capabilities enable the distinct
observations presented in this study. We then analyze the transient
dynamics and spectral features of PeNCs dispersed in toluene solvent
under non-reactive conditions. Subsequently, we explore the in situ
photoinduced substitution process, examining changes in the
bromide-to-chloride ratio and their effects on the ultrafast transient
absorption spectra of charge carriers. For the next target, we investi-

temporal changes as the nanoplatelets aggregate into higher-order
structures. In addition to presenting novel photophysical insights from
these two experiments, we demonstrate that AI-TA is a powerful
technique for rapid DAQ, enabling in situ ultrafast spectroscopy to
monitor processes occurring over extended timescales.
Results and discussion
Asynchronous and interferometric transient absorption (AI-TA)
spectroscopy
Numerous attempts have been made to reduce the DAQ time asso-
ciated with transient absorption, one of the most widely used third-
order nonlinear spectroscopy techniques. Re ﬂecting on past initia-
tives, such as the adoption of array detectors and computational data
reconstruction, we can identify two key rate-determining factors
1,35,36:
ﬁrst, the generation of pump-probe time delays using linear stages,
and second, the execution of data averaging to reduce noise levels.
AI-TA overcomes the limitations imposed by conventional tech-

mode-locked lasers. When the two lasers have slightly different repe-

repetition rates (Fig. 1a), referred to as the detuning frequency ( Δf ).
This method ensures consistent spatial overlap of the pump and probe
beams, regardless of the duration of the time delays. The equation

emitters

Through an iterative fabrication approach, often referred to as
compositional engineering, remarkable strides have been achieved in
developing ef ﬁcient perovskite solar cells
58–61 and light-emitting
devices62. This concept also extends to the quantum yield ef ﬁciency
of PeNCs55. The importance of halide composition has been empha-
sized in studies highlighting the close link between the purity of a
single-photon source and its halide composition
63. Halide exchange,
usually induced by salt-based mechanisms, has been a topic of great
interest for those who study the effects of compositional modi ﬁca-
tions while preserving morphology and minimizing other structural
inﬂuences
43,47,54,64. In particular, chloride substitution, despite its
favorable bandgap for blue or ultraviolet light sources, has faced
challenges in practical applications due to low quantum yield and
relatively poor power conversion ef ﬁciency
51,65. Although composi-
tional engineering has proven to be effective, it remains a time-
consuming and complex process. As a result, considerable efforts have
been directed toward evaluating photoluminescence lifetimes
through in-line synthesis
66. Our strategy, utilizing AI-TA, offers a faster
and more precise method for halide composition engineering.
AI-TA measurement of photon-driven transformation process
In the next phase of our AI-TA investigation, we observed changes in
the transient features of PeNPLs dispersed in hexane as the measure-
ment progressed. PeNPLs are characterized by stronger exciton
binding energy due to enhanced quantum conﬁnement from thickness
control. The thickness is quanti ﬁed by the number of lead halide
octahedra layers, referred to as monolayers (MLs), in the quantum-
conﬁned dimension. In addition to varying the halide composition
mentioned earlier, the bandgap energy of PeNPLs can also be tuned by

3 is
~7 nm, and the size of a cubic unit cell is 0.58 nm 13,31,67.
The composition investigated here consists of cesium lead bro-
mide with a 2 ML conﬁnement layer. This is the thinnest variant, other
than 1 ML, which consists of a single layer of lead halide octahedra
without cesium cations and is stabilized with ligands. A TEM image
conﬁrms the formation of PeNPLs with an approximate size of 20 nm in
the non-conﬁned dimension (Fig.5a), which is known not to affect the

68. The absorption and emission spectra of the

reported values, whereas bulk materials with the same composition
show peaks near 530 nm
68,69. The sharp excitonic peak con ﬁrms the

additional peaks in the longer wavelength region (Fig. 5b). The red-

higher-order PeNPLs with more MLs, indicating the occurrence of
photon-driven transformation during the AI-TA measurement.

Spectra of transient signals at a ﬁxed tpump-probe of 1 ps (Fig. 5e)
and a ﬁxed probe wavelength of 431.6 nm (Fig. 5f) were collected to
compare the evolution of the signals over reaction time, revealing clear
and deﬁnite changes. The shifts in the PB signals to lower wavelengths
are subtle but noticeable in the AI-TA spectra. The bandgap bleach
peak shifts by ~1 nm, accompanied by changes in the distribution of
excited carrier populations, as indicated by shifts in both sidebands
(Supplementary Fig. 17). This effect becomes more pronounced when
comparing normalized spectra acquired at different reaction times.
This observation can be attributed to the preferential degradation of
PeNPLs with larger non-conﬁned dimensions. However, the impact of
this parameter on the shift of the excitonic absorption peak is less
signiﬁcant compared to the number of layers, which serves as a more
discrete parameter
68 (Supplementary Fig. 18).
The collection of time proﬁles at aﬁxed wavelength (Fig.5f) shows
that the decay trend also changes. The triexponential ﬁto ft h et i m e
proﬁles yields three different time constants (Supplementary Fig. 19),
which can be interpreted in terms of kinetics similar to those identiﬁed
earlier in Fig. 2, representing hot carrier thermalization, charge trap-
ping, and carrier recombination70.
The shortest component, corresponding to the hot carrier ther-
malization process, provides a unique insight into the dynamics of
PeNPLs. The spectral and temporal signature comprises a sub-
picosecond peak redshift, appearing as a decay at shorter wave-
lengths and as a rise at longer wavelengths. The excess energy of the
hot state is lost via electron-phonon coupling. As the measurement
progresses, the hot carrier relaxation lifetime of PeNPLs gradually
increases from ~0.08 to 0.12 ps, indicating a bottleneck in the relaxa-
tion dynamics.
Although the hot phonon bottleneck is reported to have a negli-
gible impact on highly conﬁned CsPbBr
3 PeNCs71, such a slowdown in
hot carrier cooling has been observed in superlattice PeNPLs 72.S i m i -
larly, the efﬁciency of hot phonon cooling is much better in colloidal
samples compared to ﬁlm counterparts with the same number of
MLs73. In both cases, carrier cooling has been compared between col-
loidally dispersed and dried samples and con ﬁrmed through power
dependence measurements. Another study on a sample aged for
80 days and measured with time-resolved upconversion spectroscopy
also reports an increased lifetime
33.
Likewise, our results can be interpreted as an agglomeration-
induced suppression of hot carrier relaxation. The excess energy of the
hot state is dissipated via electron-phonon coupling to form long-
itudinal optical phonons
72,74. The thermal energy is subsequently
transformed into out-of-plane modes and dissipated into the envir-
onment, particularly ef ﬁciently in highly con ﬁned small PeNCs and
PeNPLs. However, the formation of stacked structures, known as
superlattices, suppresses this out-of-plane coupling and causes a bot-
tleneck in thermal relaxation. In our case, the observation of the hot
phonon bottleneck was achieved not by measuring power depen-
dence, but through fast DAQ of the progressing photoinduced
agglomeration of PeNPLs.
The other lifetime, associated with the charge-trapping process,
remains almost consistent. This lifetime is assumed to be intrinsic to
the state of PeNPLs undergoing AI-TA measurement, where femtose-
cond laser pulses create a photochemically dynamic and highly stres-
sed environment. Another interesting observation is that the lifetimes
of the longest component are also increasing. This component reﬂects
exciton recombination, which may involve trapped charges, as
observed in the case of PeNCs. This could be related to the size
reduction observed alongside the PB peak shift, which involves the
removal of incomplete unit cells with vacancies at the edges of the
nanoplatelets.
This trend can also be visualized in collections of highly aver-
aged and normalized time pro ﬁles at longer wavelengths. One
advantage of AI-TA is that it allows control of the length of DAQ for
averaging, enabling us to validate the minute changes observed here.
Shorter acquisition times result in a lower signal-to-noise ratio, so
integrating longer reaction times and analyzing the data over these
periods helps clarify the trend observed in the experiment. This is
demonstrated by averaging over different reaction times. Comparing
the averaged results for 1, 5, and 10 min of t
react (Supplementary
Fig. 20) conﬁrms the observations made with 1-min averages. Again,
we emphasize the strength of the AI-TA technique, particularly its
ability to account for changes occurring throughout the measure-
ment process.
Discussion
In this study, we successfully applied the AI-TA technique to the
in situ observation of the photophysical behavior of perovskite
nanomaterials undergoing photoinduced chemical reactions and
transformation processes. We investigated specialized forms of light-
induced photodegradation and demonstrated that, in some cases,
the measurement process itself can in ﬂuence the results of a spec-
troscopic experiment. Our AI-TA technique helps elucidate the
impact of such measurement effects. This method offers a stream-
lined approach for investigating photoinduced dynamic processes
across a broad temporal range, from femtoseconds to minutes. By
conceptualizing the time taken for the experiment as a chemical
reaction axis, this technique can be regarded as an unconventional
form of multidimensional spectroscopy. While this experiment
focused on perovskite nanomaterials, the methodology holds pro-
mise for extension to other photoreactive chemical or biological
systems, thereby expanding the scope of its applicability.
In summary, the ﬁrst study presented here enhances our under-
standing of the relationship between trap states and chloride-
to-bromide variation in CsPb(Br/Cl)
3 P e N C sa saf u n c t i o no fr e a c t i o n
time and provides an effective strategy for investigating similar sys-
tems. It is worth noting that both experimental veriﬁcation and theo-
retical calculations of halide composition variations would typically
require substantial resources and time investment. The AI-TA techni-
que effectively addresses these challenges by reducing several months
of investigation to just a few minutes, while requiring only a small
amount of material for multiple compositions. The second study
involving PeNPLs represents an interesting example of bridging pho-
tophysical observations between ﬁlms and colloidal nanoplatelets.
This study offers a deeper understanding of the excited-state dynam-
ics and spectral shifts that occur as colloidally dispersed particles
aggregate. With the emergence of advanced data handling technolo-
gies, where the acquisition of extensive datasets for analysis is crucial,
our work stands to make a meaningf ul contribution to the future of
materials research.
Methods
Asynchronous and interferometric transient absorption (AI-TA)
spectrometer
The outputs of second-harmonic generation from two Ti:Sapphire
mode-locked lasers (Rainbow2, Femtolasers) were used as funda-
mental light sources, serving as the pump and probe lasers, as well as
the radiation sources for photo-substitution reactions of PeNCs. BBO
crystals (Castech) with different critical phase matching conditions
were used to convert the laser source wavelength from the near-
infrared to the near-ultraviolet region. Their repetition rates were
stabilized to 80.0 MHz for the probe and 80.0 MHz + Δf for the
pump by phase-locking to an 8-channel frequency synthesizer
(HS9008B, Holtzworth) referenced by a GPS-disciplined Rb atomic
clock. The detuning frequency, Δf , was set to 51.2 Hz, 153.6 Hz, or
Article https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-60313-3
Nature Communications|         (2025) 16:4956 10
460.8 Hz (8 fs, 24 fs, or 72 fs time steps, respectively) depending on
the measurement window of pump-probe time. The digitizer was
operated at 80.0 MHz, synchronized with the frequency of the probe
pulses, to record light intensity within a preset time interval. The
second-harmonic generation signal, produced by the pump and
probe overlap on a nonlinear crystal, was used as an optical trigger
that established the starting point of decay proﬁles. Pump and probe
pulses were focused using UV-enhanced aluminum off-axis parabolic
mirrors at a 1 mm sample cell (21/Q/1, Starna Scienti ﬁc). The cell
contained a sample and was vigorously stirred using a magnetic bar.
This stirring serves the dual purpose of minimizing the photo-
degradation and the photothermal signals while expediting the
equilibrium for anion exchanges, which occur rapidly enough to be
considered simultaneous
18. After passing through the sample, the
interferogram of the probe pulse was acquired using a balanced
photodetector (PDB415A, Thorlabs) in a symmetric con ﬁguration75.
Chirp compensation is performed post-measurement to correct for
dispersion at early time delays (<100 fs) (Supplementary Fig. 21).
Every experiment was conducted under ambient, room-temperature
conditions. MATLAB with embedded function packages was used to
analyze data, including the FFT. A more detailed instrumental and
theoretical description of the method is provided in Supplementary
Notes and Supplementary Fig. 22.
Chemicals
Lead acetate trihydrate (Pb(CH3COO)2.3H2O, 99.99%), cesium carbo-
nate (Cs 2CO3, reagent Plus, 99%), lead(II) bromide (PbBr 2, ≥98%),
benzoyl bromide (C6H5COBr, 97%), benzoyl chloride (C6H5COCl, 98%),
acetone (CH 3COCH3, HPLC, ≥99.9%), toluene (anhydrous, 99.5%),
hexane (C 6H14, ≥99%), chloroform (HPLC Plus, ≥99.9%), octadecene
(ODE, technical grade, 90%), oleylamine (OLAM, 70%), and oleic acid
(OA, 90%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. All chemicals were
used without any further puriﬁcation.
Synthesis
CsPbX3 (X=Cl, Br) perovskite nanocrystals.C s P b X3 (X=Cl, Br) PeNCs
were prepared by following the reported procedure 76 with slight
modiﬁcations. In a typical synthesis, cesium carbonate (16 mg), lead
acetate trihydrate (76 mg), 0.3 mL of OA, 1 mL of OLAM, and 5 mL of
ODE were loaded into a 25 mL 3-neck round-bottomﬂask and degassed
under vacuum for 1 h at 100 °C. Subsequently, the temperature
increased to 170 °C under Ar, and 0.6 mmol of the mixture of benzoyl
chloride/bromide (a precursor ratio of 1:1) was swiftly injected. The
reaction mixture was immediately cooled down in an ice–water bath.
Finally, 5 mL of toluene was added to the crude NC solutions, and the
resulting mixture was centrifuged for 10 min at 3500 rpm. The super-
natant was discarded, and the precipitate was redispersed in 5 mL of
toluene for further use.
2ML CsPbBr
3 perovskite nanoplatelets .A l l - i n o r g a n i cP e N P L s
with the composition CsPbBr 3 were synthesized using a previously
reported ligand-assisted reprecipitation method under ambient
conditions
68. Two precursors were prepared prior to conducting the
synthesis. One was a solubilized lead bromide (0.01 mmol) in a mixture
of 0.1 mL of oleylamine, 0.1 mL of oleic acid, and 10 mL of toluene. The
mixture should be stirred and heated at 100°C until PbBr
2 powder is
fully dissolved. The cesium-oleate precursor was prepared by dissol-
ving 0.1 mmol Cs
2CO3 in 10 mL of oleic acid. This was also stirred and
heated at 100 °C until fully dissolved. The ratio of precursors to anti-
solvent in the synthesis determines the thickness of the synthesized
PeNPLs. In the case of 2ML PeNPLs, 0.15 mL of Cs-oleate precursor was
added to a vigorously stirring 3 mL of PbBr
2 precursor. Immediately,
2 mL of acetone serving as an antisolvent was injected, and the mixture
was kept stirred for 1 min. Then the solution was transferred to a 50 mL
conical tube and centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 3 min. The supernatant
was discarded, and the precipitate was redispersed in 2 mL of hexane.
All PeNPL solutions used for AI-TA experiments were kept for no
longer than 2 weeks after synthesis.
Steady-state absorption and emission spectroscopy
The absorption and emission spectra of nanocrystals were acquired
using Lambda 465 (Perkin Elmer) and Duetta (Horiba), respectively.
A quartz cell with a path length of 10 mm was used for the mea-
surement, and the sample was diluted to one-tenth of the stock
solution.
X-ray diffraction
A Rigaku D/Max Ultima III X-ray diffractometer with graphite-
monochromatized Cu Kα (λ = 1.54056 Å) radiation was used to iden-
tify the crystal structure of PeNCs (Supplementary Fig. 23). The PeNC
sample solution was drop-casted onto the substrate for measurement.
The diffractometer was set to 40 kV with a current of 30 mA, and the
spectra were collected from 20° to 60° with a 0.01° sampling width.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy
K-alpha (Thermo VG, U.K.) instrument was used to measure the XPS
spectra of the PeNCs. The PeNC samples were spin-coated on the
silicon substrate for the measurement. The wide scan and narrow scan
spectra were obtained by using a monochromatic Al X-ray source
(1486.6 eV). The energy step sizes of the survey and narrow scans were
1 eV and 0.1 eV, respectively. The binding energy of the measurement
was calibrated by the standard electron energy of 284.8 eV corre-
sponding to the photoelectron from the carbon 1s state.
Transmission electron microscopy
The estimation of PeNC size was performed using a Tecnai G2 F30ST
(FEI) microscope. For high-resolution measurement, a 300 S/TEM
(Double Cs Corrected Titan3 G2 60, FEI) equipped with ChemiSTEM
technology is used.
Time-correlated single-photon counting
TCSPC measurements were conducted using FluoTime300 (Pico-
Quant). The sample was excited with a laser with a center wavelength
of 405 nm. The photon count data was binned at 25 ps. For the stock
sample, PeNC in toluene, and the PeNC sample after the experiment,
the detection wavelength was set to 439.8 nm (5 nm bandpass) and
419.8 nm (5 nm bandpass), respectively.

ABSTRACT
Asynchronous and interferometric transient absorption (AI-TA) spectroscopy is a powerful technique for probing ultrafast dynamics, offering
both time-resolved insights and frequency-domain information with a single-point detector. In this study, we successfully measured the
transient absorption signal of rod-shaped tellurium microcrystals under low pump fluence using a mid-infrared (MIR) AI-TA setup. By
leveraging exceptionally stable frequency combs for both the pump and probe beams, coherent averaging in the MIR AI-TA enabled the
clear observation of transient absorption signals, even in heterogeneous samples under low pump fluence. The standard deviation of the TA
signal decreases with averaging time (τavg)following a 1/√ τavg dependence, confirming the ergodicity of the TA measurement over extended
averaging periods. These results highlight the significant potential of MIR AI-TA spectroscopy for advancing our understanding of ultrafast
carrier dynamics in MIR-active materials.

I. INTRODUCTION
Transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy is a versatile time-
resolved technique for investigating photoinduced reactions, energy
transfer processes, and carrier dynamics in semiconducting
materials.1–3 However, conventional TA methods are limited by
mechanical time-delay scanning, which restricts the scanning range
and introduces temporal instability. Asynchronous optical sam-
pling (ASOPS)-based TA addresses these limitations by detuning
the repetition rates of two mode-locked lasers, enabling auto-
matic time-delay scans. 4–13 ASOPS-based TA has been applied to
nanometrology,10–12 thickness metrology of layered semiconduc-
tors,13 marker-free biosensing, 5 and the investigation of ultrafast
carrier dynamics in semiconductors.9,14
We have further advanced this approach by developing a novel
asynchronous and interferometric transient absorption (AI-TA)
measurement technique, 14–16 enabling frequency-resolved TA
measurements through the incorporation of a self-referenced
scanning Mach–Zehnder (MZ) interferometer positioned after the
sample.14 In the self-referenced MZ interferometer depicted in
Fig. 1(a), the optical phase-scanning stage operates orthogonally
to the waiting time scanning process of the AI-TA system, where
the latter is determined by the repetition rate difference between
the pump and probe combs. 17 This configuration allows AI-TA
to capture frequency-resolved TA signals across a broad temporal
range, from femtoseconds to nanoseconds. Unlike conventional
TA methods, which rely on a monochromator integrated with
a point detector or a spectrograph integrated with a charge-
coupled device (CCD) camera, AI-TA achieves time-frequency
measurements using a single-point detector. This technique has
also been successfully adapted for two-dimensional electronic
spectroscopy.18–21
Notably, AI-TA achieves an excellent signal-to-noise (SN) ratio
through coherent averaging, 22,23 even while operating with pulse

energies several orders of magnitude lower than those used in
conventional TA methods reliant on amplified lasers with
1–100 kHz repetition rates. Coherent averaging is a signal pro-
cessing technique applied to repetitive signals, 22 where multiple
datasets are averaged based on temporal consistency across rep-
etitions. This approach allows the consistent signal to add con-
structively while reducing uncorrelated noise. As the averaging time
(τavg) increases, the contribution of random noise decreases follow-
ing 1 /√ τavg dependence, reflecting the stochastic nature of noise.
However, beyond a certain threshold ( τavg > τc), systematic effects
prevent further reduction in the standard deviation, limiting the
benefits of extended averaging. In our AI-TA measurements, the use
of exceptionally stable frequency combs as radiation sources allows
coherent averaging to significantly enhance the SN ratio over pro-
longed periods. This is possible because the setup’s highly stable
lasers ensure that the ergodicity of the physical system is sustained
over long durations. Ergodicity is the property of a system in which
all accessible states are uniformly explored over time, making the
time average equivalent to the ensemble average.
In this study, we investigate the effect of coherent averaging
on enhancing the SN ratio in MIR asynchronous sampling tran-
sient absorption (AS-TA) and AI-TA measurements. We refer to
the setup as AS-TA rather than ASOPS-TA, as the pump and
probe sources operate in the infrared, outside the visible spectral
region. Using both AS-TA and AI-TA, we successfully measured
the ultrafast carrier dynamics of rod-shaped tellurium (Te) micro-
crystals at a low pump fluence of 1.28 μJ/cm2, significantly lower
than the typical fluence range of several hundred to thousands
of μJ/cm2 used in conventional TA. Despite the heterogeneity of
the Te microcrystal, in our AI-TA, TA signals in time and spec-
tral domains with a high SN ratio were routinely observed. For
example, the linear absorption spectrum of the sample in Fig. 1(b)
exhibits a flat response at 1.6 OD, indicating that scattering within
a heterogeneous sample obscures the measurement of key features
related to the semiconductor’s bandgap energy. To measure the
nonlinear response buried under the scattering noise, conventional
methods typically use much higher pump fluence compared to our
method. As a result, they may lead to sample damage or intro-
duce complications in the TA signal analysis due to the occurrence
of pump-fluence-dependent photoinduced dynamical processes. On
the other hand, in our proof-of-principle MIR AI-TA experiments
here, we used pump fluence lower than 2 orders of magnitude,
but still, we could observe ultrafast dynamics of Te microcrystals
with significant scatterings taking advantage of coherent averaging
of the temporal dynamic response signals. In addition to the non-
linear time-frequency analysis, the extensively sustained ergodicity
observed over 5 × 105 iterations in the AS-TA measurements high-
lighting its suitability for various measurement techniques requiring
high SN ratios in low fluence experiments.
II. EXPERIMENTAL METHODS
A. Experimental setup of MIR AS-TA measurement
The experimental configuration for the MIR AS-TA measure-
ment is illustrated in Fig. 1(a). The setup utilized MIR frequency
combs (FC1500-250-ULN, Menlo Systems) as both pump and probe
sources, delivering trains of pulses with a duration of 150 fs and a
center wavelength of 3300 nm [Fig. 1(c)].17 To generate femtosecond
pulses at 3.3 μm, the spectrum at 1560 nm was broadened to span an
octave (1.0–2.0 μm) using a highly nonlinear fiber. The spectral com-
ponents at 1560 and 1060 nm were then amplified and combined
in a periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN) nonlinear crystal via
difference frequency generation (DFG), producing a 3.3 μm MIR
frequency comb with a zero carrier–envelop offset (CEO) frequency.
The residual lasers from the DFG process were used to generate
optical triggers through sum-frequency-generation (SFG).
The repetition rates of the MIR pump comb ( fr + Δ fr) and
probe comb ( fr) were synchronized by phase-locking to radio fre-
quency (RF) reference frequencies at their 4th harmonics. This was
accomplished by supplying reference RF frequencies at 4 fr for the
probe and 4( fr + Δ fr) for the pump, generated by a multichannel
RF synthesizer (HS9008A, Holtzworth). The synthesizer’s time base

B. Experimental setup of MIR AI-TA measurement
The asynchronous sampling method was employed for
pump–probe time delay scanning in AI-TA, similar to the AS-TA
measurement. In addition, a self-referenced interferometer 14 was
incorporated, as depicted on the right side of Fig. 1(a), positioned
after the sample to acquire TA spectra. During the t-scan with the
asynchronous sampling method, the probe interferogram was simul-
taneously scanned by continuously moving the translational stage at
a constant speed ( τ-scan). By moving the translational stage slowly
enough to minimize its impact on the t-scan profile, two orthogo-
nal time-domain datasets were obtained, a technique referred to as
two-fold time multiplexing (TTM), 16 as illustrated in Fig. 2(b). The
mechanical stage and its motion controller used for the τ-scan are
XMS-50 and XPS D-3, respectively, manufactured by Newport.
The t-scan, which changes the pump–probe time delay, was
repeated at intervals of 1 /Δ fr with the asynchronous sampling
method. With a moving stage, the interferogram was recorded with
an autocorrelation step size of 1 /Δ fr during the t-scan process.
Under these conditions, the effective step size of theτ-scan was given
by Δτ= 2v
c ⋅ 1
Δ f , where v is the stage speed and c is the speed of
light. With the stage scanned at a speed of 100 μm/s, this resulted
in Δτ= 0.23 fs. In this measurement, the mechanical stage scans
240 μm, resulting in 2.4 s of τ-scan time.
The stage speed should be carefully chosen, taking into account
the Nyquist frequency and stage recoil. To prevent signal distor-
tion caused by aliasing, the highest spectral component of the probe,
102 THz, as shown in Fig. 1(c), should be scanned at a rate slower
than the Nyquist frequency, Δ fr/2 = 1440 Hz, during the τ-scan.
When multiplied by the downconversion factor (2v
c ), this results in a
laboratory frequency of 68 Hz. Therefore, a stage speed of 100 μm/s
satisfies the Nyquist frequency requirement. In addition, the recoil
effect should be considered. If the stage moves too rapidly, recoil
can cause instability in its motion, preventing the stage from main-
taining a constant speed and introducing distortions in the inter-
ferogram. To minimize this effect, the stage should operate at an
optimal speed. For this scan, the optimal speed was determined
to be 100 μm/s.
Fast Fourier transform (FFT) was applied to the interferograms
to obtain the TA spectra. The FFT was performed on interferograms
recorded at different time points in the t-domain. By acquiring mul-
tiple AI-TA datasets and applying coherent averaging, TA spectra
with a high SN ratio were obtained [Fig. 2(b)].

IV. DISCUSSION
A. Low-fluence TA spectroscopy of semiconducting
materials
The extended coherent averaging capability of AI-TA is partic-
ularly advantageous for experiments conducted at low pump fluence
compared to conventional TA. In conventional TA measurements
with a single amplified laser combined with a translational stage,
the data acquisition time for each measurement is prolonged due
to the use of lasers with kHz repetition rates. For instance, in a
setup combining a monochromator and a single point detector, TA
signals for each spectral component are obtained by repeatedly scan-
ning the pump–probe time delay and then averaging the results.
In contrast, when using a spectrograph coupled with a CCD cam-
era, the spectral data are repeatedly collected at a fixed pump–probe
time delay to produce an average, and this process is repeated for
different pump–probe time delays. As a result, systematic effects
such as temperature fluctuations, sample condition variability, and
laser power fluctuations introduce significant deviations in the
standard deviation of signals from the expected 1/ √ τavg behavior,
limiting the effectiveness of averaging over a sufficient number of
measurements.26 In addition, the lack of stabilization in the radia-
tion sources exacerbates these issues, further restricting averaging.
Consequently, under comparable pump fluence conditions, AI-TA
achieves a significantly higher SN ratio than conventional TA.
AI-TA measurements are advantageous for experiments that
are to be conducted at low pump fluence, where pump-fluence-
dependent processes—such as multiexciton generation 27 and Auger
recombination28—can complicate the analysis of carrier dynamics
or electron relaxation processes in semiconducting materials and
quantum dots. Moreover, the high SN ratio achieved by AI-TA facil-
itates the detection of signals from heterogeneous samples, where
conventional TA measurements are often hindered by pump scat-
tering. AI-TA is well-suited for measuring excitonic decay rates in
highly scattering materials too.
In Ref. 10, ASOPS-TA was used to measure ultrafast photoa-
coustic oscillations in InAs nanowires, demonstrating its ability to
acquire the high SN ratio signals at a relatively low pump fluence
of ∼100 μJ/cm2. The authors investigated the mechanical response
of the nanowires under pump laser excitation by experimentally
observing photoacoustic oscillations and simulating their acoustic
behavior. As conventional TA systems employing amplified lasers
can introduce nonlinear mechanical effects not accounted for in our
quantitative analyses of the experimental results with an analytical
theory of the photoacoustic phenomenon, the use of ASOPS-TA was
critical in that study.
B. Comparison with rapid-scan TA technique
Given that AI-TA allows rapid single-shot acquisition, it can
be meaningfully compared to other fast acquisition techniques used
in time-resolved spectroscopy. In the visible-to-near-infrared (NIR)
region, a fast-scanning technique has been developed by mod-
ulating mechanical delay using shakers with scan rates reaching
several tens of scans per second to enhance data acquisition effi-
ciency in time-resolved spectroscopy.29 Coherent averaging has been
employed to enhance the SN ratio, with the time delay modu-
lated over a 5 ps window in 10-fs step size using the shaker. This
technique offers a time step that is flexibly adjustable and is also
applicable to amplified laser systems operating at kilohertz repetition
rates, which prevent cumulative effects in slow-dynamics materi-
als compared to oscillator-based TA measurements. However, these
schemes do not incorporate optical triggering and are not stabi-
lized to an atomic clock, which restricts their long-term averaging
capabilities. In contrast, MIR AI-TA can achieve long-term averag-
ing by leveraging its optical triggering and stabilization based on
an atomic clock. In addition, the method used in Ref. 29 is diffi-
cult to extend to the MIR spectral region due to a lack of suitable
optical components, such as multiple sets of narrow-bandpass filters
with various center wavelengths and bandwidths narrow enough to
resolve TA signals—components that are more readily available in
the visible-to-NIR range.
C. Perspectives on the development of the AS-TA
and AI-TA methods
The AS-TA and AI-TA methods have great potential for appli-
cations in various fields. The asynchronous sampling method using
a frequency comb shows significant promise for application in
fluorescence microscopy 30,31 and stimulated Raman scattering
microscopy.32 These methods often face challenges related to pho-
todamage caused by high-fluence excitation, limiting the observa-
tion of biological systems. Integrating asynchronous sampling with

Furthermore, the MIR AI-TA enables ultrafast studies of carrier
dynamics in narrow bandgap semiconductors 25,33,34 and intraband
transitions in colloidal quantum dots.35–38 For instance, III–V semi-
conductors such as indium arsenide (InAs) and indium antimonide
(InSb), which are commonly used in MIR photodiodes 39–41 or as
components in superlattice photodiodes,42–45 are of particular inter-
est. Te microcrystals and nanowires are also attractive MIR bandgap
materials exhibiting MIR lasing properties. Given the limited num-
ber of comprehensive studies on the carrier dynamics of these mate-
rials, MIR AI-TA holds great potential. In addition, broader spectral
coverage using a tunable or broadband MIR frequency comb46,47 can
further expand its applicability.
V. CONCLUSION
In this study, we demonstrate the impact of coherent averag-
ing on the SN ratio improvement under exposure to extremely low
pump fluence in MIR AS-TA and AI-TA measurements. The stan-
dard deviation of the AS-TA measurements decreased from 3× 10−4
to 2 × 10−6 with increasing averaging times up to 173.6 s, while that
of the AI-TA measurements decreased from 4 × 10−4 to 2 × 10−5
with averaging times up to 3080 s. The exceptional stability of the
mid-IR frequency combs used as pump and probe sources ensured
ergodicity over extended averaging periods, significantly enhancing
the SN ratio of TA signals, even for heterogeneous samples and low
pump fluence. This MIR AI-TA setup holds great promise as a pow-
erful tool for investigating MIR-active materials, providing deeper
insights into the development of MIR optoelectronic devices. More-
over, the asynchronous sampling-based approach using frequency
combs offers the potential for expansion into microscopic tech-
niques targeting systems highly susceptible to photodamage. This
potential arises from their ability to perform coherent averaging
while maintaining sustained ergodicity, paving the way for broader
applications in the future.

ABSTRACT: Since the advent of time-resolved spectroscopy based on
precision frequency technology of laser sources, it has been considered an
alternative way to study dynamic processes in photochemical systems.
This Perspective introduces asynchronous and interferometric nonlinear
spectroscopy (AI-NS), a spectroscopic technique that combines
asynchronously generated laser pulses and interferometric detection,
offering an unprecedented temporal dynamic range with high spectral
resolution and rapid data acquisition capabilities. By eliminating the need
for mechanical delay stages, AI-NS facilitates the rapid collection of time-
resolved data on dynamics ranging from femtoseconds to nanoseconds
while simultaneously distinguishing frequency-dependent responses.
Here, we detail the technical methodology of AI-NS and explore its
applications to the studies of various systems, including semiconductors and biological systems. Additionally, we highlight
prospective advancements, such as integration with multidimensional spectroscopy techniques. AI-NS not only expands the scope of
spectroscopic analysis but also opens new avenues for the exploration of diverse materials and molecular systems.
I. INTRODUCTION
Spectroscopy utilizing two or more pulsed lasers has been
steadily advancing, though at a slower pace compared to its
single-laser counterparts. The technical complexity in the initial
setup likely hindered broader interest and adoption in the
scientific community. In 1987, asynchronous optical sampling
(ASOPS) was first introduced and subsequently established as
a term encompassing techniques that perform pump−probe
spectroscopy using a pair of mode-locked lasers without a
linear delay stage.
1,2
In this scheme, the temporal delay
between pulses is automatically generated by the difference in
the repetition rates of the laser sources.
Over the years, the ASOPS technique has evolved to
incorporate various sources with repetition rates reaching
GHz,
3−5
enabling investigations of a variety of targets,
including semiconductors and biological systems.
6−9
The
technique has also been applied across broad electromagnetic
spectral regions, covering X-ray,
10
deep ultraviolet,
11
near-
infrared,
12
mid-infrared,
13
and terahertz spectroscopies.
14,15
Notable advantages of the ASOPS technique include rapid data
acquisition capability, low energy per pulse, consistent overlap
of pump and probe pulses over extended delay times, which
facilitates coherent averaging, and a broad temporal scan
range.
12,16
While the ASOPS method originally emerged as a time-
resolved technique for detecting pump-induced responses, a
similar approach�dual-comb spectroscopy (DCS)�can be
used for frequency-resolved linear spectroscopic measure-
ments.
17−19
In DCS, coherent interactions between collinearly
propagating, phase-stabilized frequency comb outputs with
slightly detuned repetition rates generate time delays and
produce interference.
20
Unlike ASOPS-based nonlinear spec-
troscopy, DCS requires precise locking of the carrier-envelope
offset (CEO) frequency, making it a coherent counterpart of
ASOPS.
21,22
Consequently, ASOPS applications in pump−
probe spectroscopy can be considered incoherent ASOPS.
23
Given the extensive information available from both the time-
and frequency-resolved measurements, there is a clear need for
a technique that integrates both domains−this is where our
asynchronous and interferometric nonlinear spectroscopy (AI-
NS) comes into play.
As mentioned earlier, numerous dynamics studies have been
conducted using ASOPS pump−probe spectroscopy. In this
approach, the probe response is detected using a single-point
detector, which inherently lacks frequency-resolving capabil-
ities in its basic configuration. This setup can pose challenges
in analyzing data of nonfrequency-resolved ASOPS transient
absorption (ASOPS-TA), especially when attempting broad-

Another important consideration is that the TA signal may
display negative changes in optical density, indicating increased
probe beam intensity due to processes such as bleaching or
stimulated emission (SE). Without wavelength-selective
detection, these negative absorption signals could cancel out
positive excited state absorption signals (ESA), resulting in a
diminished overall signal. Although filters or monochromators
can isolate specific spectral responses, maintaining the fast data
acquisition advantage of ASOPS requires equally rapid
frequency-resolved detection, where interference-based scan-
ning can be beneficial. Furthermore, correcting for group
velocity dispersion across different wavelengths becomes
challenging when using multiple filters. To address these
issues, our group has been developing and refining a
spectroscopic technique termed AI-NS, an advanced pump−
probe spectroscopic tool built on the ASOPS frame-
work.
8,13,16,24
Theoretical descriptions and technical details of AI-NS were
comprehensively covered in previous reviews and tutorials
provided by our group.
23,25,26
In this Perspective, we begin
with a detailed introduction to AI-NS instrumentation and
general theory, followed by an overview of advanced
techniques. We also present demonstrations of AI-NS
applications in studying biological and chemical photo-
dynamics, along with a summary of various ultrafast dynamics
that can be investigated using this method. Finally, we discuss
the prospects of AI-NS, highlighting potential improvements
and enhancements.
II. BASICS OF ASYNCHRONOUS AND
INTERFEROMETRIC NONLINEAR SPECTROSCOPY
II-1. Asynchronous Optical Sampling (ASOPS). In
conventional nonlinear spectroscopy using a single mode-
locked laser, a train of output pulses is first separated by a
beamsplitter, and the time delay between them is controlled by
adjusting the path length difference, typically using a
mechanical translation stage. In simple pump−probe spectros-

However, maintaining consistent beam

II-2. Interferometric Detection. The spectral analysis of
the probe in a conventional system typically uses a fixed
pump−probe time delay while the probe spectra are measured
and averaged using spectrographs. Such systems may include a
monochromator with a lock-in amplifier, a spectrograph with a
CCD, or a temporal interferometric scan of the probe with a
linear stage. However, in ASOPS, the time delay continuously
varies, adjusting the pump−probe delay with each pulse pair,
rendering averaging at fixed delays impossible. The continuous
change in time delays, driven by oscillator outputs at MHz or
higher frequencies, demands a detection scheme capable of
operating at similar rates. In such cases, the measurement
involves fixing the probe frequency-related dimension while
scanning the pump−probe time delays, as illustrated in Figure
1b. It is possible to incorporate this step with a continuously
moving stage. This methodology is called time-division
multiplexing,
24
which can be applied when the signal input
in a single channel is modulated across different time scales,
allowing data analysis in different temporal segments to reveal
distinct information. The orthogonality of the two time
variables is ensured by the scale difference between the
responses. The key point is that the scanning speed remains
constant, and the probe modulation induced by the interfero-
gram scan is much slower than that induced by the pump
pulses. These are the essential components in performing AI-
NS or AI transient absorption (AI-TA) measurements. The
interferogram can then be Fourier-transformed to extract
spectral information.
The interferogram is generated by the arrival delay of split
probe pulses. If the probe beam is split before incidence on the
sample, the interferogram can resolve phase information. This
type of interferogram generation with a noninteracting probe
pulse called a local oscillator (LO) is known as the asymmetric
detection method.
17
In contrast, if the probe beam is split after
incidence on the sample and then interfered, it is considered a
self-referenced detection of the interferogram, as shown in
Figure 1c. Therefore, the spectral analysis in ASOPS is akin to
fixing the probe-LO delay or the probe−probe delay, and then
scanning the time-dependent response. To proceed, the
sampling points of the interferogram should be evenly spaced.
This can be achieved using periodically generated trigger
signals with a temporal interval of 1/Δf (Figure 1d).
