II-3. Coherent Averaging and Trigger Generation.
The ergodicity of AI-NS allows consecutive measurements to
be averaged over time, enhancing the signal-to-noise ratio
(SNR). The start of each recurring measurement can be
marked by trigger generation, which indicates the spatial and
temporal overlap of the pump and probe pulses. Defining the
zero time of the pump−probe delay requires a method for
determining coincident timing, which can be achieved in
several ways. One approach is to use electronic trigger
generation, where coincidence detection of each pulse is
monitored by a fast photodiode.
1
Alternatively, an electronic
correlation signal can be generated through two-photon
absorption of a photodetector.
14
We present two methods of
optical trigger generation, both of which involve taking a
portion of each beam from RSML using a beamsplitter and
redirecting it for optical trigger generation. The first uses
collinear propagation of the two beams to generate
interference, similar to the approach used in DCS.
24
This
produces a sharp interference signal minimizing jitter to 2 fs
using 7 fs pulses while requiring a smaller amount of energy
than those generated by nonlinear interactions (Figure 2a).
However, this optical trigger signal based on the interference
fringes is found to be more susceptible to jitter due to the
fluctuation of input beam intensities from noise. The second
trigger generation method involves sum-frequency generation
using a nonlinear crystal, such as beta barium borate (BBO).
By noncollinearly crossing the two pulses from different
RSMLs and focusing them at the BBO, the intensity
correlation signal of sum-frequency is used for the optical
trigger in this case, resulting in background-free signals. Using
appropriate voltage amplifiers and filters increases the signal
and helps filter out unwanted noise, resulting in improved jitter
performance and achieving subfemtosecond precision for a pair
of 7 fs pulses (Figure 2b).
The trigger generation interval corresponds to the inverse of
the detuning frequency (1/Δf). It is recommended to match
the path length difference between the two RSMLs at the
points of trigger generation and the sample interaction. To
facilitate this, a retroreflector mounted on a linear stage can be
incorporated to adjust the path length difference. This
alignment ensures that the trigger signal coincides with the
time zero of the pump−probe delay. Careful attention should
be paid to this aspect, especially when using a fast digitizer, as
the device processes raw data steps relative to the trigger signal.
Also, additional time delays in electronic circuits in the signal
processing path require caution as well, as they can affect
timing accuracy.
The detected trigger signal should include a sufficient
number of sample points at a fixed sampling interval to avoid
missed triggers caused by inevitable time jitter, which is a
critical factor in determining time resolution. When a large
detuning frequency is applied, it may result in an effective
sampling interval so long that the temporal overlap between
two pulses does not occur. To generate a trigger signal with
time steps longer than the initial pulse duration, intentional
chirping can be introduced before trigger generation to
temporally broaden the pulse and enable overlap. This can
be achieved by placing a parallel fused silica window in the
beam path and using a thicker BBO crystal to extend the
propagation length and satisfy phase-matching conditions.
II-4. Electronic Detection Scheme. After the photo-
detector, the signal passes through a voltage amplifier and a
low-pass filter designed to block the laser’s fundamental
frequency (e.g., a 48 MHz low-pass filter for 80 MHz
repetition rate lasers). This filters out high-frequency
oscillations in the down-converted radio frequency region,
enabling the detection of slowly varying signal components
without distortion. A similar effect can be achieved by using a
detector with a low bandwidth.
In addition, when using an AC detector, it is important to
take into account the impact of the lower side of the cutoff
frequency.
28
If the cutoff frequency is set too high, accurate
detection could become difficult or even impossible. In terms
of laboratory time, if the transient responses last longer than
the inverse of the AC cutoff frequency, the decay may appear
to be completed earlier than it actually is, leading to an
underestimation of the lifetime.
When employing AC detectors with high cutoff frequencies
on the order of kHz, the linear stage should move rapidly to
avoid interferogram distortion. However, this fast movement
can introduce undesirable effects, as stated earlier in section II-
2. Therefore, the frequency specifications of other detection
components, such as voltage amplifiers and fast digitizers,
should also be carefully evaluated to ensure optimal perform-
ance.

often weak and require a high-resolution digitizer, particularly

III. RELATED TECHNIQUES AND ADVANCEMENTS
III-1. Frequency Upconversion/Downconversion. One
characteristic of the RSML output is that the stability of the
repetition rate remains unchanged during the frequency
conversion process. This principle is fundamental in stabilizing
the CEO frequency in DCS using an f-2f interferometer, which
compares coherence transferred to the supercontinuum and
the second harmonic of the fundamental source to generate a
reference for phase stabilization.
20,29
The ability to transfer
these characteristics to upconverted or downconverted comb
components while maintaining the stability of the repetition
rate of fundamental outputs is highly advantageous for various
applications (Figure 4a).
30
Experimentally, by evaluating the
stability of the repetition frequency of laser outputs at
converted wavelengths, a similar stability of repetition
frequency could be observed in both up-converted and
down-converted wavelengths.
We have developed and demonstrated this approach with
various RSML sources across broad bandwidths. For instance,
the second harmonic generation of the fundamental output can
produce near-ultraviolet (NUV) sources from the initially near-
infrared (NIR) region of Ti:sapphire output.
16
Similarly,
intrapulse difference frequency generation (DFG) can be
used to obtain a supercontinuum in the mid-infrared (MIR)
region while retaining a frequency-stabilized comb structure.
31
Difference-frequency-generated RSML sources offer an addi-
tional advantage: passive phase stabilization. This occurs
intrinsically because the CEO frequency of MIR frequency
combs generated by the DFG process is to be zero in principle.
The time interval stability of RSML can be assessed by
measuring Allan deviation of the repetition rate, which reflects
the timing stability between laser pulses over increasing
integration time scales. In ASOPS and other time-precision
techniques, the periodicity of the signal is utilized for obtaining
averages in a process called coherent averaging.
This approach can be compared and contrasted with
methods where multiple targets are simultaneously presented
and measured to perform averaging in numbers. In such
numerical averaging, it is assumed that the constituents
contributing to the average are identical. In comparison, for
time averaging, or coherent averaging, it is assumed that
measurements taken at different times are identical and
consistent�this is the principle of ergodicity.
In such cases, conventional statistical representations such as
standard deviation are insufficient, as they only reflect the
distribution of signals relative to an overall average. Allan
deviation addresses this issue by grouping the data set into
segments of equal length, calculating the averages of each
segment, and measuring the variance and the standard
deviation of the adjacent averages. The expectation value of

AI-NS-based measurement of 2D-ES offers several advan-
tages, including shorter data acquisition times and the ability to
eliminate artifact signals. The low energy per pulse,
approximately 1 nJ, helps minimize higher-order nonlinear
responses, such as those originating from multiexciton
generations, and removes scattering contributions through
double FFTs. In the future, the dimensionality of the AI-NS
measurement could be further extended by integrating other
multipulse techniques or incorporating additional laser
sources.

It is noted that a trade-off exists between the time resolution
and duty cycle in ASOPS and AI-NS systems using RSMLs
with identical repetition rates, as temporal and spatial overlap
only occurs every 1/Δf. In other words, achieving higher time
resolution results in a lower duty cycle and longer data

acquisition times due to the need for averaging. Once the TA
signals complete decay, the pump−probe pulse pairs before the
next overlap are considered insignificant data, thereby
prolonging acquisition. Although this time can be utilized−
for example, by using shutter control to cool down and prevent
the destruction of molecular species−it inevitably introduces
dead times that do not contribute to data collection. In this
regard, using two lasers with different repetition rates offers a
significant advantage: more frequent trigger generation.
Additionally, for AI-NS, this allows for more frequent sampling
of interferograms, enabling a higher maximum stage speed and,
consequently, faster data acquisition.
IV. PERSPECTIVE AND A FEW CONCLUDING
REMARKS
In the future, the strategy for a more efficient and rapid
collection of frequency- and time-resolved responses using our
AI-NS is expected to drive significant advancements in
nonlinear spectroscopy. Based on the discussions presented
in this Perspective, we can outline a vision for the future of AI-
NS. First, the use of supercontinuum and frequency conversion
promises to expand the spectral range of investigations.
Additionally, incorporating time-division multiplexing and
performing multipulse spectroscopy could enable new types
of nonlinear spectroscopic measurements. The use of more
than two mode-locked lasers is also a viable option. Finally,
data acquisition rates can be further enhanced by employing
RSMLs with different repetition rates.
The vision presented in this work can be drawn with the
techniques and efforts demonstrated in DCS and ASOPS-TA,
which could open new avenues of research with AI-NS. For
instance, the development of broadband frequency-stabilized
sources, such as supercontinuum generation and other spectral
broadening methods, has been explored and utilized in several
DCS studies.
49,50
Depending on the target system under investigation or the
desired data acquisition speed, an appropriate repetition rate
can be chosen and optimized. Faster data acquisition is
achievable with RSMLs featuring high fundamental repetition
rates, reaching hundreds of GHz and beyond, as demonstrated
before.
3,5
On the other hand, a common challenge in studying
diverse photochemical systems is the need to allow long-lived
decay processes to complete and dissipate accumulated heat
before the arrival of the next pump pulse. A potential solution
to this challenge is pulse-picking, which reduces the repetition
rate by increasing the pulse-to-pulse interval, thereby extending
the observable temporal window.
51
Other problems and limitations associated with ASOPS also
apply to AI-NS, such as the need for precise control of the
repetition rate and the acquisition of unnecessarily detailed
measurements over longer time scales. However, postmeasure-
ment correction of time delays has been shown to be feasible
in arbitrary detuning ASOPS, even without the synchroniza-
tion of two lasers.
52,53
In such cases, the use of regeneratively
amplified outputs and electrical tuning becomes possible. For
the latter, modulating the detuning frequency to scan only the
temporal region of interest can truncate insignificant data at
longer delays, thereby enhancing data acquisition rates.
54,55
Additionally, the significant constraint of requiring two lasers
has been addressed in some cases by using a single cavity laser
to perform DCS.
56−58
Looking ahead, we anticipate similar advancements for AI-
NS. Dedicated efforts to refine and expand AI-NS techniques
hold considerable promise, positioning it as a compelling and
innovative approach likely to capture the attention of
spectroscopists worldwide.

ABSTRACT: Rod-shaped tellurium microcrystals are promising mid-infrared photonic materials and a prototypical chiral (Weyl)
semiconductor, yet intrinsic band-edge relaxation at room temperature is often masked by hot-carrier and photothermal pathways
under above-gap excitation. Here, we employ mid-infrared asynchronous and interferometric transient absorption (MIR AI-TA)
spectroscopy with frequency-comb pulses centered near the band-edge (380 meV) to directly interrogate two band-edge resonances.
The time- and frequency-resolved AI-TA data reveal a fast component characterized by a time constant of 1−2 ps and a long-lived
component with a time constant of ∼50 ps, common to both resonances. A global spectro-temporal model assigns the fast
component to phonon-assisted redistribution of valence holes coupled to recovery of pump-induced Peierls distortion, while the
slow component corresponds to band-edge electron−hole recombination. These results demonstrate that MIR AI-TA can
quantitatively disentangle coupled electronic and structural dynamics in narrow-bandgap semiconductors.
I
norganic materials that absorb mid-infrared (MIR) photons
have garnered significant attention due to their potential
applications in telecommunications, photodynamic therapy, IR
detectors, and IR emitters.
1−4
These materials are particularly
promising for optoelectronic applications, prompting extensive
research into exciton recombination processes in colloidal
quantum dots
5
and narrow bandgap chalcogenide semi-
conductors.
6
Elemental tellurium (Te) crystal has emerged as
a standout material in this context. Te atoms form covalent
bonds in a trigonal helix structure, with these helices assembled
into a hexagonal structure by van der Waals interactions
(Figure 1a). This crystal structure gives rise to a bandgap
energy of approximately 0.33 eV
7
(Figure 1b) and endows the
material with unique properties such as optical nonlinear-
ity,
8−10
thermoelectricity,
11−13
photoconductivity,
14,15
and
piezoelectricity.
16
In addition, it is also utilized as a
prototypical Weyl semiconductor for the study of topological
quantum matter.
17−20
Importantly, Te microcrystals and nanowires have recently
emerged as promising platforms for MIR photonics, exhibiting
strong MIR emission and even lasing properties at cryogenic
temperatures.
21,22
In particular, rod-shaped Te microcrystals
have demonstrated intense MIR lasing at cryogenic temper-
atures due to internal cavity modes, with a reported quality
factor of 40.7.
22
This remarkable behavior arises from the
unique combination of Te’s exceptionally high refractive index
(∼4.8) and its microrod morphology, which supports efficient
resonant cavities through whispering gallery modes (WGMs).
To utilize this promising material in practical MIR emitters
and photodiodes operable under ambient conditions,
23
it is
essential to gain a detailed understanding of its ultrafast carrier
dynamics, especially near the band-edge at room temperature
(RT).

Several studies have explored the ultrafast carrier dynamics
of Te crystals near the band-edge using near-infrared (NIR)
pump-MIR probe techniques.
24−27
However, accurately
probing these band-edge dynamics requires careful exper-
imental design, especially in the selection of pump wavelength.
Processes such as intervalley scattering, photothermal effects,
and carrier multiplication can contribute to the transient
absorption (TA) signal and complicate its interpretation.
24−27
For example, in our previous work
25
and the study by Jnawali
et al.,
26
NIR pump-MIR probe measurements were conducted
to investigate carrier dynamics and spectral features around
Te’s bandgap. Although these measurements captured carrier
dynamics in different valleys - such as the H-valley and L-valley
- they made it difficult to isolate and interpret electron−hole
recombination at the H-point band-edge.
Furthermore, under NIR excitation, a significant portion of
the absorbed energy is dissipated as heat due to the cooling of
hot electrons from higher-lying conduction bands down to the
band-edge. As a result, photothermal effects can significantly
contribute to the TA signal, further obscuring the interpreta-
tion of intrinsic carrier dynamics.
28
Even in more recent
pump−probe studies on Te nanoflakes using a pump centered
at 2 μm and a probe at 4 μm, photothermal contributions
remain non-negligible, despite the suppression of intervalley
transitions.
24
Carrier multiplication, which arises when the
pump photon energy exceeds the band gap, can also generate
multiple excitons and further complicate signal analysis.
29,30
To
address the complication due to nonlinear processes, Maly ́ et
al. suggested an intensity cycling to separate the single particle
signal from the multiparticle signal in TA measurement.
30
Pump fluence should also be carefully controlled. At high
photoexcited carrier densities, nonradiative Auger recombina-
tion becomes the dominant relaxation pathway. For example,
Zhuo et al.
24
reported that in a 100 nm-thick Te nanoflake
excited by a 2 μm pump pulse with fluences ranging from 20
μJ/cm
2
to 80 μJ/cm
2
, Auger recombination predominated.
Such high fluence generates high carrier concentrations,
potentially obscuring the intrinsic optical properties of
tellurium.
To unambiguously investigate the intrinsic band-edge carrier
dynamics, we employ asynchronous and interferometric
transient absorption (AI-TA) spectroscopy using degenerate
MIR optical frequency combs centered at 3262 nm (0.380 eV)
(Figure 1c).
31
This technique utilizes the exceptional stability
of frequency combs to implement the asynchronous sampling
(AS) method,
32,33
where a slight detuning in repetition rates
between the pump and probe pulses automatically scans the
pump−probe time delay. Simultaneously, the probe interfero-
gram is scanned via a self-referenced interferometer to resolve
the spectral information.
25,31,34
By tuning the photon energies resonant with the H
6
CB
→H
4
transition and maintaining low pump fluences (0.89 − 1.28)
μJ/cm
2
, corresponding to photoexcited carrier densities
(n
carrier
) of (7.79 − 11.2) × 10
15
cm
−3
(Supporting Note
3B), we minimize contributions from higher-order recombi-
nation channels. The high signal-to-noise (SN) ratio under
weak excitation was made possible by extended coherent
averaging, resulting from the exceptional stability of the MIR
frequency combs and precise timing control via optical
triggers.
31
Specifically, our measurements also captured the recovery of
pump-induced Peierls distortion. While previous studies have
also noted structural dynamics in tellurium, such as Gatti et
al.’s report on a bandgap shift driven by coherent A
1
optical
phonons
35
and Jnawali et al.’s observation of ultrafast band
splitting attributed to coherent longitudinal acoustic pho-
nons,
26
our work advances this understanding by establishing a
quantitative physical model. A global analysis of the full AI-TA
data set yields good agreement with experiment, detailing the
coupled carrier and lattice dynamics near the band edge.
Consequently, this study provides a clear view of the
radiative behavior of rod-shaped Te microcrystals, offering
valuable insights for their implementation in ambient-operating
MIR optoelectronic devices. Furthermore, by elucidating the

In this work, we have identified two primary relaxation
pathways in rod-shaped Te microcrystals using degenerate
MIR AI-TA spectroscopy: radiative recombination and thermal
redistribution of holes, coupled with Peierls distortion
recovery. Analysis using the kinetic model reveals that the
fast component (time constant of 1−2 ps) is attributed to A
1
phonon-assisted process, while the slow component (time
constant of ∼ 50 ps) corresponds to band-edge electron−hole
recombination. Spectral analysis further reveals that the hole
redistribution process is coupled to Peierls distortion recovery.
Moreover, the global analysis quantitatively reproduces both
the bandgap shifts and carrier relaxation processes. These
results elucidate the ultrafast photophysics of Te microcrystals,
paving the way for their application in MIR optoelectronic
devices and advancing Weyl semiconductor research.

Layered Ruddlesden–Popper perovskite (RPP) photovoltaics have gained substantial attention owing to
their excellent air stability. However, their photovoltaic performance is still limited by the unclear real-
time charge-carrier mechanism of operating devices. Herein, we report the correlation between the
charge-carrier mechanism and the spatially heterogeneous RPP bulks induced by distinct sublattice
cations in the state-of-the-art antisolvent-driven RPP devices. In particular, abnormal heterogeneities
ranging from the lateral long-range to local sub-grain scale and corresponding charge-carrier
behaviours are visualized for triple-cation RPPs. We discovered that such heterogeneities with a unitary
2D/3D hybrid suppress lattice vibrations and reduce Fro ¨hlich interactions by about 2 times, significantly
promoting charge-carrier dynamics. Consequently, optimized triple-cation RPP solar cells greatly
outperform their mono-cation counterparts. Furthermore, this principle can be applicable irrespective of
2D layer thickness ( n 4 2) and substrate type. This work provides a rationale for leveraging a disordered
structure to stimulate charge-carrier motion and suggests the design principle of low-dimensional
perovskites.
Broader context
Solar cells using layered Ruddlesden–Popper perovskites (RPPs) as active layers have demonstrated promising long-term stability to approach industrial
application. Different from the traditional phase-pure three dimensional perovskites, the peculiar spatial heterogeneous phases within RPPs mak e the charge-
carrier mechanism ambiguous especially when the device is working. Here, we demonstrate a systematic way to tune and understand the correlation betw een
the charge-carrier mechanism and the spatial heterogeneities in efficient RPP solar cells. We visualized the presence of abnormal heterogeneities from the
lateral long-range to local sub-grain scale with a unitary 2D/3D hybrid, which contributed to an improved charge-carrier dynamics with reduced Fro ¨hlich
interactions in triple-cation RPPs. Such principle can enhance device performance irrespective of 2D layer thickness ( n 4 2) and substrate type. The designed
spatial heterogeneities offer unique opportunities to advance the layered RPP devices.

Introduction
Organic–inorganic perovskites have emerged as promising
alternatives to traditional photovoltaic semiconductors, 1–8
owing to their excellent optoelectronic properties. 9–12 Despite
the substantial progress in device performance using perovskites,
the stability issue has not been resolved yet. This can be attributed
to their high ionic mobility and the related ion migration.
13–15
Two-dimensional (2D) perovskites have been recently
reinvestigated to address the instability against open air, which
entails the introduction of bulky ammonium cations along
certain crystal planes.
16–19 Bulky organic spacers allow less
ion migration between crystal planes to stabilize devices. 20 In
addition, 2D layer can modify 3D perovskite surface to adjust
interfacial energy level, thus favoring for higher device
efficiency.
21 Ruddlesden–Popper phases (RPPs) are the most
prevalent 2D structures with a general formula of
(A)
2(B)n/C01PbnI3n+1, where A is a bulky ammonium cation, B is
a small cation and n is the number of [PbI 6]4/C0units.17,22,23
Theoretically, an ordered quantum well regime in RPPs
imposes strong in-plane exciton binding energies and limits
charge transport in solar cells.
24,25
To achieve a high eﬃciency in RPP photovoltaics, investigating
reproducible lattice compositi ons at the molecular level and
understanding the underlyingoperando mechanism at the device
level are prerequisite. Hot-casting methods have been proposed to
overcome the limited charge transport and achieve eﬃcient RPP
solar cells.
22 However, production up-scaling and reproducibility
still remain challenging due to the diﬃculty of pure stoichio-
metric polycrystalline RPP film formation, where a 2D/3D hybrid
forms inevitably.
25,26 To this end, eﬀorts have been dedicated to
produce and regulate RPP phases without hot-casting, such as
antisolvent methods.
27–30 In addition, the lessons learned from
traditional 3D perovskites suggest that triple cation lattices
possess an enhanced structural st ability and improved charge-
carrier dynamics. In this scenario, the triple cation engineering is
expected to be a reproducible way to control over the RPP lattices
by antisolvents.
31–33 Importantly, energy transfer from low- to
high-dimensional phase was suggested to be responsible for the
charge-carrier mechanism in the fabricated RPP films. 34–37
Nevertheless, such measuremen ts only limited to RPP films
cannot fully address the correlation between the charge-carrier
mechanism and spatial phase heterogeneity in a real device. The
mechanism of energy transfer, both between separate grains and
within a grain, remains unclear for efficient RPP solar cells. Thus,
the fundamental understanding of RPP solar cells severely lags
behind the continuously improving device efficiency.
In this study, we identify and further investigate the fundamental
correlation between the charge-carrier mechanism and spatial
perovskite heterogeneity in eﬃcient antisolvent-driven RPP
devices. Here, triple-cation-based RPPs (henceforth referred to
as CsFMRP) and mono-cation-CH
3NH3
+-based ones (denoted as
MRP) were employed to allow diverse spatial hierarchical
compositions. During device operation, real-time visualisation
of the spatial charge-carrier distribution and local phase verified
an abnormal heterogeneity with a unitary 2D ( n = 3)/3D hybrid,
from the lateral long-range to local sub-grain scales, in bulk
CsFMRP. Furthermore, the observed 3D-like phases arising from
the sub-grains governed the charge-carrier collection of the
corresponding device. In contrast, the MRP devices exhibited a
complex behaviour assisted by multiple 2D-like phases (hybrid
low dimensional perovskite with various n values) together with
limited 3D-like phases. Such abnormal heterogeneity in CsFMRP
was proven to suppress lattice vibrations, thereby lowering
carrier–lattice interactions. We discovered that the heterogeneity
can enhance device efficiency irrespective of the choice of 2D
layers (n 4 2) and substrate type. Accordingly, an optimal solar
cell efficiency of 16.15% was achieved using CsFMRP ( n =4 ) .
Our findings offer a fundamental perspective on the charge-
carrier mechanism in highly efficient RPP solar cells.

Conclusions
Unlike traditional homogeneous photoactive layers, the triple-
cation RPP films present a complex local structure, with spatially
heterogeneous multi-dimensional phases, which had so far
hindered a complete understanding of the fundamental
charge-carrier dynamics in working devices. We propose a
comprehensive strategy by examining real-time charge-carrier
behaviour, analysing charge-carrier dynamics and correlating
the mechanism with spatial phases at multiple length scales.
For the RPPs yielding high device performance, the charge-
carrier behaviour and the assigned abnormal heterogeneity of
structural phases were identified from the lateral long-range to
local sub-grain scale with a unitary 2D/3D hybrid, rationalizing
the lattice vibration dependent energy transfer mechanism. We
foresee that the visualized peculiar abnormal heterogeneity of
solution-processed RPPs will aﬀect the fundamental understanding
of low dimensional perovskite photovoltaic devices as well as other
hybrid semiconductors with multis cale structures. Finally, this
work will provide insights regarding both compositional design
and charge-carrier engineering forfuture applications of organic–
inorganic perovskites.

Device fabrication
ITO substrates (25 mm /C225 mm) were cleaned sequentially
using acetone, isopropanol, and deionized water. Then, the
substrates were dried in a nitrogen flow, and treated by
UV-ozone for 20 min. Before perovskite deposition, PTAA
solutions (1.5 mg mL
/C01 in toluene) were spin coated at
6000 rpm for 30 s. The coated substrates were annealed at
100 1C for 10 min. Perovskites were fabricated as described
previously. Finally, the substrates were moved to a vacuum
chamber for evaporation deposition of 20 nm C
60, 6 nm BCP,
and 80 nm Cu films at a rate of 0.2 Å s /C01. For the flexible
devices, 50 mm-thick polyethylene(naphthalate) (PEN) films
were used as flexible substrates and PEDOT:PSS (Clevios
PH1000) was used for transparent conductive electrode. PEN
substrates were treated by O
2 plasma and subsequently PH1000
was spin coated at 4000 rpm for 40 s. The flexible devices were
completed by annealing at 120 1C for 15 min, followed by
cooling for 3 min; no further annealing was required.

A metal aperture mask was used to define the active area as
7.29 mm
2. A standard silicon cell (91150-KG5, Newport) was

simulated solar spectrum using 100 mW cm
/C02 radiation from a

density–voltage curves were obtained using a Keithley 2400,
from /C00.1 to 1.2 V in forward scan and from 1.2 to /C00.1 V in
reverse scan. The scan rate was set as 100 mV s /C01 with a delay
time of 200 ms. To validate device performance, the scan rate
was varied from 10 to 2000 mV s
/C01. A homemade EQE system
with a Xenon lamp (75 W; USHIO Ltd, Japan) was used to record
the EQE spectra. To investigate the stability of the output, the
current density was recorded continuously at the MPP voltage
determined from the J– V scan. All characterization experiments
were conducted in a glovebox at room temperature.

A 500 MHz SSNMR system (Bruker Advance III HD, Bruker,

Characterization of TAS
TAS was conducted using a regeneratively-amplified Ti:Sapphire
laser (Hurricane, Spectra-Physics) with the output wavelength
centred at 800 nm, an energy of 0.55 mJ per pulse, full-width-at-
half-maximum of 130 fs, and 1 kHz repetition rate. We generated
400 nm pump pulses by passing the source pulses through a
second harmonic generator (TP-1A, Spectra-Physics) with a
power of 20 mW. Probe pulses were obtained by focusing the
800 nm light using a UV-fused silica planoconvex lens (CVI
Melles Griot, f = 100 mm) onto a 3 mm sapphire plate
(WG30530, Thorlabs). The angle between the polarisation of
the pump and the probe was set to 54.7 1 to exclude polarisation
eﬀects. The time delay between the pump and the probe pulses
was scanned using a linear stage (M-414.3PD, Princeton Instru-
ments). The pump pulses were modulated using an optical
chopper (MC1000, Thorlabs) synchronised to the trigger from
the source laser. The probe pulses of the signal were detected by
photodiodes (2031, New Focus) after wavelength selection using
a monochromator (250 IS/SM, Chromex, 600 grooves mm
/C01
grating blazed at 750 nm). TAS signals were obtained using a
lock-in amplifier (SR830, Stanford Research Systems).

A UV-visible spectrophotometer (Cary 5000 UV-Vis-NIR, Agilent

QM-3/2004SE (PTI) from a TAS system. The PL quantum yield
was obtained by mounting an integrating sphere in the PL
spectrofluorometer. Top-view SEM images were acquired using

profiles, including height, conductivity, and deformation, were
simultaneously measured using an atomic force microscope

various enhanced conducted AFM modules. A Raman spectro-
meter (T64000, Horiba Ltd, France) was used to analyze the
lattice vibrations using 532 nm laser excitations, where the
samples were encapsulated by glass and sealed with epoxy.
XRD patterns over the range of 0 1 to 601 2y were obtained using
a high-resolution system (SmartLab, Rigaku Ltd, Japan) with Cu
Ka radiation. Grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering was
conducted using a Xeuss 2.0 HR SAXS/WAXS system (France)
with an exposure dwell time of 60 s. An electron spectroscopy
instrument (AXIS SUPRA, Kratos Ltd, United Kingdom) was used
to measure both XPS and ultraviolet photoelectron spectra (UPS),
calibrated by an incident radiation using the He I peak
(21.22 eV). For temperature-dependent PL, a spectrofluorometer
(FlouTime 300, PicoQuant, Germany) was used to measure
PL spectra with changes in temperature using 520 nm laser
excitations.

ABSTRACT: Herein, we report signi ﬁcant ﬂuorescence
quenching induced by intramolecular photoinduced electron
transfer (PET) in electron donor −acceptor-type π-conjugated
organic molecules with methoxy-containing donor moieties.
The ﬂuorescence quenching of the diketopyrrolopyrrole
(DPP, a well-known highly emissive luminophore) derivatives
seemed to be a ﬀected by the methoxy moieties. Steady-state
optical properties of the synthesized materials were analyzed
in the solution, aggregate ( N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone/H
2O),
and solid states in order to understand the in ﬂuence of the
surrounding environment. The mechanistic aspect of the
intramolecular PET process in methoxy-containing DPP
derivatives was revealed by singlet oxygen generation
measurements and ultrafast femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy. These results could provide crucial insights
toward designing emissive π-conjugated organic molecules.
1. INTRODUCTION
π-Conjugated organic molecules are a fascinating class of
luminescent materials for optical and electronic applications as a
result of their high tunability characteristics through the
modiﬁcation of chemical structure; they are also generally less
expensive than inorganic materials.
1 In recent times, π-
conjugated organic luminescent molecules have been utilized
in a wide range of applications that require highly emissive
properties in the solid stat e, such as luminescent solar
concentrators (LSCs), 2 organic light-emitting diodes
(OLEDs),3 optical storage,4 and chemosensors.5 In this context,
eﬀorts have been made to enhance the ﬂuorescence quantum
yield (Φf)o f π-conjugated organic luminescent molecules in the
solid state by reducing nonradiative decay channels such as
aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ), energy transfer, and
charge separation.6−8
The methoxy group, an electron-donating group that contains
a lone pair of electrons, has been commonly introduced into π-
conjugated organic luminescent molecules in order to induce
the red shift of the absorption and emission spectra.
Interestingly, signi ﬁcant ﬂuorescence quenching as well as the
red shift of optical spectra was reported recently in some
electron donor (ED)−acceptor (EA)-type π-conjugated organic
molecules containin gm e t h o x yg r o u p s .9−12 However, the
mechanism of ﬂuorescence quenching has not yet been clearly
unraveled. Earlier, our group observed unexpected and excep-
tional ﬂuorescence quenching in a diketopyrrolopyrrole (DPP)
derivative containing methoxy groups in the ED moieties. 13
Considering that DPP is a well-known highly emissive
luminophore,
14,15 the ﬂuorescence quenching appeared to be
signiﬁcantly a ﬀected by the methoxy moieties. Therefore,
herein, we attempted to verify the mechanism of ﬂuorescence
quenching by methoxy groups in π-conjugated organic
molecules.
We assumed that the intramolecular photoinduced electron
transfer (PET) process, which is one of the photodeactivation
processes,
16,17 played a key role in ﬂuorescence quenching in
ED−EA-type π-conjugated organic molecules containing
methoxy groups. In order to verify our assumption, a series of
ED−EA-type DPP derivatives were designed and synthesized,
which were either methoxy-containing or methoxy-free.
Fluorescence quenching was observed only in DPPs with a
triphenylamine (TPA) donor containing methoxy groups,
whereas strong ﬂuorescence was seen in DPPs with a
methoxy-free TPA donor. Computational calculations were
carried out to explore the feasibility of intramolecular PET in the

HOMO electrons of MTPA could be transferred more easily
to the HOMO of DPP rather than BTPA because of their higher
HOMO level, which is contributed by nonbonding n states.
Figure 3 shows the electron density distributions of the

Gaussian 09 program package). Detailed calculation results
including oscillator strength performed via TDDFT (B3LYP/6-

3.6. Transient-State Optical Properties. Femtosecond
TA measurements were carried out to investigate the ultrafast
intramolecular PET process. TA spectra and their temporal
proﬁles monitored at diverse wavelengths of the synthesized
materials are shown in Figure 8 a−h. The concentration of
synthesized materials was 10
−4 mol/L in THF. All of the samples
were excited with a 400 nm pump, which is considered to induce
excitation of only the DPP acceptor, as shown in Figure S6, and
probed with supercontinuum light in the wavelength range of
520−950 nm. The background signal was indicated as −1 ps.
Table 6 describes the globally ﬁtted lifetimes of synthesized
materials in TA measurements by using a triexponential
function. As shown in Figure 8a−h, TA results of all compounds
displayed generally similar spectra with negative ground-state
bleaching (GSB) signals in the wavelength range of 520 −550
nm and stimulated emissions (SE) in the wavelength range of
550−700 nm. Also, new excited-state absorption (ESA) arising
above 700 nm was observed as positive signals. Signi ﬁcant
evidence of an intramolecular PET process could be found by
comparing SE signals of methoxy-containing M1 and M2 and
methoxy-free D1 and D2. As shown in Figure 8e,f, M1 initially
displayed strong SE signals after excitation by the pump laser,
which decayed to zero in extremely short time scales (1.07 ±
0.18 ps ( t
2)). M2 also showed rapid SE decay on a time scale
similar to M1, as shown in Figure 8g,h. ESA signals of M1 and
M2 lasted longer than their SE signals. However, the transient
signals of both D1 and D2 lasted far longer than M1 and M2, as
shown in Figure 8 a−d. Especially their long SE signals lasting
over our measurement window show trends matching with their
long ﬂuorescence lifetimes and high ﬂuorescence quantum
yields.
Figure 9 describes the schematic energy diagram based on
results of TA measurement in (a) methoxy-free D1 and D2 and
(b) methoxy-containing M1 and M2. IC and VR represent
internal conversion and vibrational relaxation, respectively.
Compared to SE signals of D1 and D2, as shown in Figure 9a,
drastic decay of SE signals in M1 and M2 can be interpreted as a
result of an intramolecular PET process, as shown in Figure 9b.
Because reductively transferred electrons from the n state of
MTPA occupied the S
0 state of DPP, the SE signals
corresponding to the transition from the S 1 to S0 state of DPP
disappear as the ground state of the acceptor is occupied.
Therefore, the disappearance of intense SE signals in M1 and
M2 before ∼5 ps indicates rapid depletion of the lowest singlet
state of donor−acceptor compounds. Besides, it is assumed that
the initial ESA signals are mainly contributed to by not only S
1 to
Sn transitions but also by DPP anion radical (DPP *−) and
triphenylamine cation radical (TPA *+) signals after charge
separation by the PET process (the DPP anion radical absorbs
between 600 and 800 nm, and the TPA cation radical absorbs
between 650 and 750 nm).
40,41 Because the ESA signals showed
broad and overlapped absorptions, it was di ﬃ cult to isolate
which process has a major contribution to them. In summary, we
can conclude that the methoxy groups in M1 and M2 played a
key role in ﬂuorescence quenching via an intramolecular PET
process.

Highly Efficient Hole Transport Layer-Free Low Bandgap 
Mixed Pb–Sn Perovskite Solar Cells Enabled by a Binary 
Additive System
Hongki Kim, Jong Woo Lee, Gi Rim Han, Yu Jin Kim, Su Hwan Kim, Seong Keun Kim, 
Sang Kyu Kwak,* and Joon Hak Oh*
The development of high-performance hole transport layer (HTL)-free perov-
skite solar cells (PSCs) with a simplified device structure has been a major 
goal in the commercialization of PSCs due to the economic advantage of low 
manufacturing cost. Unfortunately, low bandgap (Eg) mixed Pb–Sn perov-
skites, which have promising utility for constructing efficient all-perovskite 
tandem solar cells, have rarely been explored in simplified HTL-free device 
configurations. In this study, efficient band bending and defect engineering 
at the interface between perovskite and indium tin oxide (ITO) are realized 
via a binary additive system using copper thiocyanate (CuSCN) and glycine 
hydrochloride (GlyHCl). Using mixed Pb–Sn perovskites decorated with 
crystalline p-type CuSCN, the energy level alignment at the hole extractive 
interface is modulated in favor of hole extraction, simultaneously increasing 
hole mobility. Suppressed nonradiative carrier recombination in the perovskite 
bulk, or across the charge extractive interface, is further achieved by GlyHCl 
without disturbing the efficient hole transfer characteristics. Notably, a more 
optimized band alignment is achieved at the hole extractive interface with the 
addition of GlyHCl. The HTL-free mixed Pb–Sn PSC shows an efficiency up to 
20.1% under forward bias with negligible hysteresis, comparable to state-of-
the-art high-performance full-structured mixed Pb–Sn PSCs.

1. Introduction
Single-junction lead-based perovskite solar cells (PSCs) 
with a typical stoichiometry of ABX 3  (A = Cs, CH 3 NH3 , or 
NH2 CHNH2 ; B = Pb; and X = I, Br, or Cl) have shown unprec-
edented achievements in power conversion efficiency (PCE), 
reaching 25.5%.
[1]  Despite these advances, there have been 
some concerns regarding the utilization of hole transport 
layer (HTL) materials, such as poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophen

been based on PEDOT:PSS, which is vulnerable in terms of 
long-term stability,[13–18]  there is an urgent need to eliminate the 
use of PEDOT:PSS as the HTL and develop efficient HTL-free 
mixed Pb–Sn PSCs.
Recently, McGehee et al. reported that the mixed Pb–Sn perov-
skite itself produces upward band bending near the interface 
with ITO, providing a PCE comparable to that of a full-structured 
device,
[11]  which is different from the behavior of conventional lead-
based counterparts.[5–7]  This notable report shows the great poten-
tial of HTL-free mixed Pb–Sn PSCs, even without electrode modi-
fication for dipole tuning across the electrode/perovskite interface, 
for implementing high-performance HTL-free mixed Pb–Sn 
PSCs. Nevertheless, the PCEs of HTL-free mixed Pb–Sn PSCs 
still lag far behind full-structured mixed Pb–Sn PSCs, without pro-
viding a methodology to obtain breakthrough efficiency.
One of the key lessons from the case of lead-based perov-
skites, in terms of improving the efficiency of HTL-free PSCs, 
is that the incorporation of p -type molecules into perovskites, 
such as copper iodide (CuI),
[6 ] copper thiocyanate (CuSCN), [19]  
and fluorinated tetraarylbenzo[1,2-b :4,5-b ′]dipyrrol-1,5-yl 
alkanediylsulfonate salt (BDPSO), [20]  can induce suitable band 
alignment for hole transfer, which helps improve the efficiency 
of HTL-free PSCs. More specifically, it is desirable to promote 
hole transfer from perovskite to ITO (i.e., decreasing hole trans-
port barrier (ΔE
h)) and block electron transfer from perovskite to 
ITO (i.e., increasing electron transport barrier (Δ Ee)), and this 
can be realized by shifting the Fermi level (E Fermi) of the perov-
skite closer to that of ITO while maintaining the upward band 
bending. However, additive systems using only p-type molecules 
raise doubts about whether such a single additive system can 
provide optimized methodologies for realizing highly efficient 
HTL-free PSCs, because efficient operation of HTL-free PSCs 
requires not only suitable band alignment, but also suppression 
of active defects at the perovskite/hole extractive interface. Non-
radiative recombination at the interface can have a significant 
detrimental effect on device performance. Furthermore, selective 
passivation of donor or acceptor defects within E
g of perovskites 
can modu late EFermi of perovskite, which implies that band align-
ment tuning via defect control in HTL-free PSCs is also feasible. 
This effect may be more pronounced in mixed Pb–Sn perovskite 
due to the lower defect tolerance compared to pure lead halide 
perovskites. Recently, Hu et al. have demonstrated the successful 
modification of the buried interface of Pb–Sn perovskite layers 
using GlyHCl additive, providing insight into the effect of band 
alignment and charge carrier recombination at the perovskite/
hole extractive interface.
[21]  Therefore, it is important to explore 
the promising use of GlyHCl additive systems for HTL-free 
mixed Pb–Sn PSCs. Unfortunately, the single-additive systems 
applied in lead-based perovskites have not provided insight into 
the effects of defect engineering on band alignment and charge 
carrier recombination at the perovskite/hole extractive interface 
in HTL-free device configurations. Therefore, it is important to 
find more advanced additive systems in single-additive platforms 
that have not been explored in HTL-free mixed Pb–Sn PSCs.
In this study, simultaneous engineering of band bending 
and defects for optimized hole transfer in a mixed Pb–Sn 
perovskite-based HTL-free device configuration was explored. 
A facile and highly effective binary additive system composed 
of CuSCN and glycine hydrochloride (GlyHCl) was applied in 
mixed Pb–Sn perovskites to facilitate hole transfer and simul-
taneously alleviate the trap-mediated nonradiative charge 
recombination that can occur in the perovskite bulk or across 
the hole extractive interface. With the incorporation of p-type 
CuSCN into perovskites, the mixed Pb–Sn perovskites were 
decorated with crystalline p-type CuSCN, resulting in greater 
hole mobility (μ
h) and a more optimized band alignment near 
the interface with ITO for hole extraction. The extended hole 
channels produced by crystalline p-type CuSCN, possibly deco-
rating the grain boundaries (GBs) of perovskite, significantly 
improved the device performance. The resulting CuSCN-incor -
porated HTL-free mixed Pb–Sn PSCs showed a much higher 
PCE (18.6%) than reference HTL-free PSCs (14.7%). Further 
improvement of PCEs was achieved by introducing GlyHCl 
salts into CuSCN-doped mixed Pb–Sn perovskites. Defect pas-
sivation of perovskites was achieved by the introduction of 
GlyHCl salts, suppressing nonradiative carrier recombination. 
This effect was confirmed by the lower trap density and charge 
carrier dynamics, where the GlyHCl-introduced perovskite 
films induced markedly longer radiative charge recombination 
lifetimes, without disturbing the efficient hole transfer charac-
teristics. Notably, a strengthened p-type characteristic of perov-
skite was observed from the defect passivation effect of GlyHCl. 
This is important in that defect chemistry of mixed Pb–Sn 
perovskite, and its passivation strategy, can contribute to the 
modulation of E
Fermi for efficient band alignment in HTL-free 
PSCs. The nature of the band modulation by defect passivation 
was investigated by density functional theory (DFT) calculation, 
where the introduction of GlyHCl passivated the donor defect 
state of the perovskite, strengthening its p-type characteristics.
As a result, the binary additive system improved the PCE of 
HTL-free mixed Pb–Sn PSC to 20.1% under forward bias with 
negligible hysteresis, which is the highest efficiency among 
HTL-free mixed Pb–Sn PSCs reported to date. CuSCN/GlyHCl-
incorporated HTL-free mixed Pb–Sn PSCs also showed markedly 
improved device stability in a nitrogen-filled glove box, as well as 
under continuous 1 Sun illumination, compared to the reference 
HTL-free devices. Our results will contribute to the development 
of cost-effective strategies for the large-scale deployment of effi-
cient transport layer-free mixed Pb–Sn PSCs in the near future.

[19,22]  The J–V curve of the resulting 
best-performing HTL-free mixed Pb–Sn PSC with CuSCN is 
shown in Figure 1b, with a stabilized PCE at MPP and a sum-
mary of the photovoltaic parameters (Table 1). Compared to the 
reference device, all photovoltaic parameters were improved, 
especially J
sc and FF, producing a much higher PCE of 18.6% 
with a stabilized PCE of 16.6%. The effects of the amount of 
CuSCN additive on device performance are also represented by 
statistics of the photovoltaic parameters (Figure S3, Supporting 
Information), exhibiting progressive performance improve-
ment with the introduction of CuSCN additive. It is assumed 
that the crystalline p-type CuSCN/perovskite heterostructure 
in perovskite films further promotes hole transport to the ITO 
electrode, serving as additional hole extractive channels.
To further improve device performance, we focused on the 
nonradiative recombination that could occur in the perovskite 
bulk or close to the hole extractive interfaces (i.e., ITO/perov-
skite or possibly CuSCN/perovskite interfaces). According to 
previous reports,
[23–26]  the higher performance can be limited 
by the nonradiative carrier recombination occurring at the 
interface with adjacent charge transport layers. This can origi-
nate from the charge recombination between minority carriers 
in the perovskite and charges in the adjacent transport layer, 
where they may recombine on their own but can also be pro-
moted by traps in the perovskite. Accordingly, mitigating the 
nonradiative recombination losses occurring across the inter -
face with HTLs would greatly facilitate targeted improvement 
of device performance. To realize this, we applied GlyHCl 
salt as an organic passivator for perovskites into the CuSCN-
incorporated perovskite precursor solution, where the quater -
nary ammonium and chloride ions in GlyHCl are expected to 
simultaneously passivate the negatively and positively charged 
defects, respectively.
[27,28]  The J–V curve of the best-performing 
device, applied with a CuSCN/GlyHCl binary additive system, 
is shown in Figure 1c, with a PCE of 20.1% under forward bias 
and a stabilized PCE of 18.1% (Table 1). Figure S4, Supporting 
Information, shows the external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 
the best-performing device, where the J
sc calculated from the 
EQE matches the values obtained from the corresponding J–V 
curves. The statistics of the devices with different amounts 
of GlyHCl clearly showed that PCE improvements were pre-
dominantly due to progressive enhancement of V
oc (Figure S5, 
Supporting Information). The improvement of Voc was also 
reflected in device characteristic analysis results, including 
the electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS), capacitance–
voltage (C–V) measurement, and light intensity-dependent 
V
oc plots for estimating the ideality factor (n) (Figure S6, Sup-
porting Information). These results indicate greater charge 
recombination resistance (Rrec), higher flat band potential (V fb), 
and lower n, confirming the suppression of charge recombina-
tion enabled by the addition of GlyHCl. Overall, the consecu-
tive introduction of CuSCN and GlyHCl significantly improved 
the photovoltaic parameters and led to a higher and reproduc-
ible PCE distribution, as shown in Figure  1d,e, respectively. 
Improved device stability was also confirmed by device sta-
bility testing in a nitrogen-filled glove box for 1000 h (Figure 1e; 
Figure S7, Supporting Information), and under continuous 1 
Sun illumination by monitoring the stabilized PCEs at MPP 
for 100 h (Figure 1f). As shown in the figures, the introduction 
of CuSCN and GlyHCl markedly improved the device stability, 
reflected in a much slower decay in PCE, with about 90% of 
the initial PCE retained after 1000 h, as well as a much longer 
latency to 80% degradation (t
80 ) of 49.3 h under continuous 
illumination compared to the reference device (t 80  = 7 .6 h). The 
stability on perovskite films with each additive system was also 
checked using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and 
X-ray diffraction (XRD) analyses, which showed a similar trend 
to the device stability test (Figures S8 and S9, Supporting Infor -
mation). We assume that the improved stability of perovskite 
films with CuSCN and CuSCN/GlyHCl originated from the 
suppressed oxidation of Sn
2+  by additional incorporation of 
SCN- ions [29,30]  and defect passivation effects by GlyHCl. We 
excluded the possibility that these performance improvements 
were due to changes in the crystallographic, optical, and mor -
phological properties of the perovskite films, as no significant 
changes of these properties were observed with consecutive 
addition of CuSCN and GlyHCl (Figures S10–S12, Supporting 
Information). Although slight crystallographic and morpho-
logical improvements were found with additives, we consider 
that these effects are not significant enough to yield high per -
formance improvements.

- and COO - com-

(Figure  2a). The high signal intensity for the COO - component 
on the perovskite surface was presumably due to unintentional

during the sample loading process (for analysis purposes). For 
the CuSCN-incorporated perovskite film, significantly increased 
intensity of SCN
- was observed near the interface with ITO 
(Figure 2b). This observation indicated that CuSCN was mainly 
buried on the bottom surface of the film. This was confirmed 
by the appearance of S 2p peaks in XPS depth profiles near the

spectral overlap of Cu 2p
3/2  and I 3p 1/2  peaks. With reference to

thereby releasing HSCN gas during the annealing process, [31,32]

face with ITO. The buried distribution of CuSCN near the inter-
face with ITO may be beneficial for controlling the hole transfer 
properties at the perovskite/ITO interface.

from a variety of point and interstitial defects at GBs in the

the perovskite film was observed with the addition of CuSCN.

tive channels, significantly accelerating the hole transfer from 
perovskite to ITO. Furthermore, the trap-assisted nonradiative 
charge recombination in the perovskite bulk, or across the hole 
extractive interface, can be mitigated by the addition of GlyHCl.

defects, but also negatively charged ones. The reduced defect 
densities, at GBs and across the hole extractive interface, can 
suppress charge recombination.

troscopy (UPS). To probe band bending near the interface 
with ITO, which can be discerned by the relative shifts of the 
core-level XPS peaks near the interface compared to those far 
from the interface,
[11,34]  we fabricated very thin (≈ 10  nm) and 
thick (≈ 800  nm) layers of perovskite on ITO. The thickness

with ITO (Figure 3 a). This indicated that the perovskite bands 
shifted upward near the interface with ITO, corresponding 
to a previous study using mixed Pb–Sn perovskites with the 
chemical formula FA
0.75 Cs0.25 Sn0.4 Pb0.6 I3 .[11]  The upward band 
bending near the interface with ITO was also confirmed by 
a higher W
F (Figure  3b, left) and lower binding energy onset 
(Figure  3b, right) of the thin perovskite/ITO sample in the 
UPS spectra. Compared to the pristine perovskite films, the 
relative shifts for XPS peaks were reduced by 120 meV to a 
lower binding energy, from the bulk to the interface, for the 
perovskite films with CuSCN additive (Figure  3c). This was 
also reflected in the UPS spectra, which revealed smaller 
differences in W
F and binding energy onset between thin 
and thick perovskite films compared to the pristine films 
(Figure  3d). These tendencies were slightly strengthened 
with the addition of GlyHCl (Figure  3e,f). Notably, enhanced  
p-type characteristics of the perovskite with sequential addition 
of CuSCN and GlyHCl additives were observed, with gradual 
shifting of the UPS spectra in the secondary electron cut-off  
region toward the lower binding energy. Figure  3g shows the 
band diagrams, characterized by band bending across the 
perovskite/ITO interface, based on the UPS results and W
F 
of ITO (Figure  S17, Supporting Information). Interestingly, 
the energetic barrier for holes (Δ E
h) decreased from 0.37 to 
0.33  eV, while Δ Ee increased from 0.88 to 0.92  eV, with the

e and lower ΔEh across the hole 
extractive interfaces, so our results indicated that the loss of

the addition of additives. The decreased Δ Eh and increased 
ΔEe could be accompanied by enhanced p -type characteris-
tics of the perovskite with the addition of additives, as these

with the addition of additives were also verified by Hall effect

concentrations from 6.7 ×  10
17  to 1.8 ×  10 17  cm-3  with CuSCN,

2  V-1  s-1 , compared to the pris-

The DFT calculation was carried out to elucidate the effect of 
GlyHCl on the defect in mixed Pb–Sn perovskite (see Experi-
mental Section for details of the calculation). Three interstitial 
defects (i.e., I
i, Pbi, Sni), three vacancy defects (i.e., VI, VPb, VSn), 
and two substitutional defects (i.e., I Pb, I Sn) were investigated 
on the flat termination (001) surface of mixed Pb–Sn perovskite; 
these defects were known to generate deep trap states in other 
halide perovskites.
[41–43]  Through density of state (DOS) anal-
ysis of pristine and defective perovskite, we examined whether 
defect formation creates a trap state within E g. Among the 
investigated point defects, only Pb i and Sn i had donor defect 
states below the conduction band edge (Figure 4c,d), while the 
other systems only generated shallow defect states (Figures 
S19 and S20, Supporting Information). In both Pb
i and Sn i, 
the charge density distribution of the defect level was localized 
around the defect site, indicating the formation of a deep trap 
state (Figure S21, Supporting Information). Subsequently, the 
passivation effects of GlyHCl on the defect of mixed Pb–Sn 
perovskite were investigated. Surprisingly, additional GlyHCl 
doping near Pb
i and Sn i sites shifted the energy level of the 
donor state to a higher level, indicating passivation of the trap 
states.
[27,42]  The passivation effect imparted by GlyHCl was pri-
marily due to the interaction between the positively charged 
Pb
i and Sn i defect, and the negatively charged Cl - ion in the 
GlyHCl molecule (acting as a counterion). Shifts in trap states 
are also known to be a result of electron transfer from the passi-
vation molecule to the surface.
[27]  Bader charge analysis showed 
that the GlyHCl molecule transferred 0.13 and 0.14 electrons to 
Pbi and Sn i surfaces, respectively. In conclusion, DFT calcula-
tion indicated that the introduction of GlyHCl effectively pas-
sivated the donor trap states, so that the perovskite would have 
relatively enhanced p-type characteristics.
To investigate the effects of CuSCN and GlyHCl additives 
on the charge carrier dynamics of mixed Pb–Sn perovskite 
films on ITO, we performed steady-state and time-resolved 
photoluminescence (TRPL) analysis of the perovskite films 
with each additive system, as shown in Figure  5a–d. Samples 
were excited with a laser at a wavelength of 372  nm from the 
direction of the glass side, as well as from the direction of the 
perovskite surface, to comprehensively determine the charge 
carrier dynamics throughout the entire films. The upward band 
bending of perovskite near the interface with ITO resulted in 
PL quenching under excitation in the direction of the glass 
side, while the perovskite deposited on the quartz glass did 
not induce PL quenching under same excitation direction 
(Figure S22, Supporting Information). These observations 
showed that the hole transfer from perovskite to ITO occurred 
near the interface with ITO. Clearly, stronger PL quenching 
was observed for CuSCN and CuSCN/GlyHCl-introduced 
perovskite films (Figure 5a,c). The extent of PL quenching was 
increased to a greater extent under irradiation from the direc-
tion of the glass side than the perovskite surface side, which 
was attributed to the more favorable charge transport near the 
ITO. The TRPL results of the films with CuSCN and CuSCN/
GlyHCl additives reflected the efficient charge transport proper-
ties in comparison with the pristine film (Figure  5b,d), where 
the TRPL curves were fitted by biexponential decay with fast 
(τ
1 ) and slow (τ 2 ) lifetime components (Table S1, Supporting 
Information). As fast τ 1  and slow τ 2  components are related 
to the extraction of photoexcited carriers in the presence of a 
charge transporting layer and radiative recombination of car -
riers, respectively,
[26,44]  we assigned τ1  to hole injection into ITO 
and τ2  to radiative bimolecular recombination in the perovskite 
bulk, or across the perovskite/hole extractive interfaces. Under 
excitation from the direction of the glass side, we obtained 
much shorter τ
1  and τ2  lifetimes of 3.7 and 9.0 ns, respectively, 
with the CuSCN-introduced perovskite film compared to the 
pristine film (τ 1  = 12.6  ns, τ 2  = 27 .0  ns). This implied that the 
carrier extraction rate improves significantly when CuSCN is 
added to the perovskite, in accordance with the much stronger 
PL quenching. Notably, the τ
2  lifetime was increased from  
9.0 to 20.9 ns with the addition of GlyHCl, while maintaining 
a short τ1  lifetime of 3.9 ns compared to the pristine film. The 
prolonged slow τ 2  component could be attributed to the sup-
pressed nonradiative recombination via efficient passivation of 
defect states. These results were also replicated under excitation 
from the direction of the surface side, indicating that GlyHCl-
containing films showed improved τ
2  lifetimes compared to 
CuSCN-containing films. These observations confirmed the 
efficient defect passivation effects imparted by GlyHCl additive, 
without sacrificing the efficient carrier transport properties.
Femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (TAS) 
analysis was also performed to investigate the charge carrier 
dynamics. ITO/perovskite films were pumped using a 400-nm 
pulse from the glass side, to elucidate carrier dynamics 
at hole collective interfaces, and probed by a weak pulse at 
950 nm after a variable time delay. The ground-state bleaching 
(GSB) was center-featured around 950 nm in the TAS spectra, 
as shown in Figure  5e, which was ascribed to state filling 
of the conduction and valence bands. As the population of 
holes in photoexcited perovskite films is expected to decrease 
with hole transfer to ITO, the temporal evolution of GSB 
represents hole injection from perovskite to ITO. Notably, a  
significant decay in the GSB intensity of perovskite was 
observed with additives compared to that of the pristine film. 
This implied that the perovskite films in the presence of addi-
tives facilitated hole extraction, consistent with the steady-
state PL results exhibiting more fluorescence quenching. The 
decay kinetics of the GSB in perovskite films with each addi-
tive system were also obtained with their corresponding fitted 
parameters (Figure 5f; Table S2, Supporting Information). The 
fast (τ
1 ) and slow (τ 2 ) time components of the decay kinetics 
could be assigned to charge carrier trapping at perovskite GBs 
and charge carrier transfer, respectively, as described previ-
ously with a time window similar to our case.
[45]  Specifically, 
CuSCN-incorporated films showed much faster τ 2  compared 
to the pristine film, indicating that the presence of CuSCN 
in perovskite further promotes hole injection from perovskite 
to ITO. Slightly different from CuSCN-incorporated films, 
prolonged τ
1  and τ 2  were confirmed with the CuSCN/GlyHCl 
additive system. Considering the still much shorter τ 2  in the 
perovskite film with CuSCN/GlyHCl compared to the pris-
tine film, we speculated that the longer recombination times 
of charge carriers were achieved with defect passivation by 
GlyHCl.

3. Conclusion
In summary, we used a binary additive system composed of 
CuSCN and GlyHCl to simultaneously improve the charge 
transport properties and mitigate nonradiative recombination 
across the hole extractive interfaces. We demonstrated that the 
introduction of p-type CuSCN into the perovskite enabled opti-
mization of band alignment at the perovskite/ITO interface, 
accompanied by increased μ
h. This greatly enhanced the PCE 
of the pristine HTL-free mixed Pb–Sn PSC from 14.7% to 18.6% 
under forward bias. A further improvement of HTL-free mixed 
Pb–Sn PSCs was achieved by the addition of GlyHCl. GlyHCl 
efficiently passivated defects at GBs in the perovskite bulk, as 
well as those across the perovskite/hole extractive interface, 
without impeding efficient carrier transport. Furthermore, the 
defect passivation effectively modulated E
Fermi in favor of more 
optimized hole extraction. As a result, the best-performing 
HTL-free device showed a PCE of 20.1% under forward bias 
with negligible hysteresis, which is the highest efficiency for 
HTL-free mixed Pb–Sn PSCs reported to date. Moreover, the 
operational stability was markedly improved with the binary 
additive system, and t
80  was significantly longer under condi-
tions of continuous illumination compared with the pristine 
device. Our findings will facilitate the development of opti-
mized charge extraction processes in HTL-free PSCs.

(DMSO), 1,2-dichlorobenzene (ODCB), and toluene were purchased 
from Sigma-Aldrich. PCBM was obtained from EM-index. All chemicals 
were used as received without further purification.
Perovskite Precursor Solution Preparation: Mixed Pb–Sn 
perovskite precursor solutions with the chemical formula 
Cs
0.05 MA0.45 FA0.5 Pb0.5 Sn0.5 I3  were prepared by dissolving 307.3  mg of 
SnI2 , 141.9  mg of FAI, 12.9  mg of SnF 2  (as an antioxidant to suppress 
oxidation of tin), 380  mg of PbI 2 , 118  mg of MAI, 21.4  mg of CsI, and 
8  mg of Pb(SCN) 2  into DMF:DMSO (800 µL:200  µL). The CuSCN-
containing perovskite precursor solutions were prepared by dissolving 
different concentrations of CuSCN powder (5.0, 7.5, 10  mg mL
-1 ) 
in the perovskite precursor solution. Perovskite precursor solutions 
containing the GlyHCl additive were prepared by adding GlyHCl to the 
CuSCN-containing perovskite precursor solution with different molar 
proportions of GlyHCl in relation to Sn (0.5, 1, 2 mol%).
Device Fabrication: ITO-coated glass slides were sonicated sequentially 
in soapy water, deionized water, acetone, and isopropyl alcohol, and 
the substrates were then treated with UV–ozone for 20  min. The ITO 
substrates were transferred to a nitrogen-filled glovebox. The perovskite 
precursor solution was spin-coated under two-step coating conditions 
of 1000  rpm for 10 s and 3500  rpm for 40 s, and then annealed at 
100  °C for 5  min. Toluene was used as the antisolvent for the second 
spin-coating process. The PCBM solution (5  mg mL
-1 ) in ODCB was 
filtered and spin-coated onto the perovskite film at 2000  rpm for 60 s. 
Then, 20-nm-thick C
60 , 7-nm-thick BCP, and 100-nm-thick Ag layers 
were thermally evaporated under vacuum (<10 -6  mbar) in sequence 
through a shadow mask. For device fabrication of full-structured mixed 
Pb–Sn PSCs, PEDOT:PSS was used as the HTL according to the same 
procedures described for the other layers. A PEDOT:PSS dispersion 
was filtered with a 0.25-µm hydrophilic filter, spin-coated onto the ITO 
substrates at 6500 rpm for 40 s, and then dried at 150  °C for 30 min. The 
active area of the device was 0.12 cm
2 .
Film and Device Characterization: Absorption spectra were obtained 
by UV–vis spectroscopy (V-770, JASCO). Steady-state and time-resolved 
PL spectra were obtained using a fluorescence lifetime spectrometer 
(C11367-32; Hamamatsu Photonics) with an excitation wavelength of 
372  nm. ToF-SIMS (TOF.SIMS-5; ION-TOF) was operated in spectral 
mode, using a 30 keV Bi
3 + primary ion source with a current of 1 pA. A 
1  keV Cs + ion source with a current of 100 nA was used as an etching 
source. The depth profile was operated under negative polarity. The XPS 
(AXIS-HSI; Kratos) was performed on prepared perovskite films. XRD 
analysis was performed using an X-ray diffractometer (D8-Advancel 
Bruker) with Cu Kα  radiation (λ  = 1.5406 Å) at 40 kV/40 mA. UPS spectra 
were acquired on ITO/perovskite, ITO/perovskite with CuSCN, and ITO/
perovskite with CuSCN/GlyHCl films using an AXIS SUPRA spectrometer 
(Kratos), with He I (21.2 eV) used as the photon source. Binding energy 
cut-off regions were used to determine W
F by subtracting the cut-off  
energy from the He I photon energy (21.2  eV). The low binding energy 
onset region was used to determine the relative distance between the 
E
Fermi and VBM of perovskites. The conduction band minimum (CBM) 
values of perovskites were calculated by considering Eg. Scanning electron 
microscopy (SEM) images were obtained using a field-emission scanning 
electron microscope (MERLIN Compact; Zeiss). The J–V curves and solar 
cell performance were measured using a Keithley 2400 source meter 
with an AM 1.5 G solar simulator (100  mW cm
-2 ). EQE was measured 
using a solar cell quantum efficiency measurement system (QEX7; PV 
Measurements). Light intensity-dependent V
oc was determined by tracking 
Voc from J–V curves at different light intensities, where the light intensity 
was modulated by optical density filters. The dark I–V curves of hole-only 
devices with the device configuration ITO/PEDOT:PSS/perovskite/PTAA/
Au were measured for extracting trap densities and μ
h under forward bias 
using a Keithley 2400 Source Meter in the dark. The C –V measurements 
were carried out in the dark at a constant frequency of 100 kHz and an 
AC amplitude of 20 mA. The EIS was measured by IviumStat at V
oc under 
AM 1.5 G illumination (100  mW cm -2 ) and frequencies from 100  Hz 
and 10 MHz with an AC amplitude of 10 mA. Hall effect measurements 
(HL5500PC; Bio-Rad) were carried out on the perovskite films with four 
square Au electrodes thermally evaporated on the edges of perovskite 
films at room temperature. The thermal admittance spectroscopy for 
obtaining tDOS was conducted using IviumStat at 0 V bias in the dark, 
with a modulated frequency from 10  Hz to 10  MHz and AC amplitude 
of 20 mV. The device stability tests under continuous illumination were 
performed at the MPP for the unencapsulated devices in a nitrogen-filled 
glove box at a temperature of ≈ 25  °C. The voltage at MPP was obtained 
automatically by the program.
TAS Analysis: For TAS analysis, the perovskite precursor was spin-
coated on a washed quartz plate, and then encapsulated in epoxy with 
a cover glass under a nitrogen atmosphere to minimize tin oxidation. 
A regeneratively amplified Ti:Sapphire laser (Hurricane; Spectra-
Physics) with an average power of 0.46 mJ per pulse, <200 fs FWHM, 
and repetition rate of 1 kHz at 800 nm was used to generate a 400-nm 
pump pulse through second harmonic generation (TP-1A; Spectra-
Physics). The supercontinuum generated by focusing 800-nm pulses 
onto a sapphire plate (WG31050; Thorlabs) was used as the probe pulse. 
The time delay between the pump and probe was controlled using a 
linear stage (M-414.3PD; Princeton Instruments). The angle between the 
polarization of the pump and probe was kept at the magic angle (54.7°). 
The pump light was modulated using an optical chopper (MC1000; 
Thorlabs), which was synchronized to the trigger from the Hurricane 
laser. The wavelength of the probe was selected by a monochromator 
(250 IS/SM; Chromex, 600 grooves/mm grating blazed at 750 nm) with 
photodiode detection (2031; New Focus), and signals were obtained 
using a lock-in amplifier (SR830; Stanford Research Systems).
Calculation Details: Spin-polarized DFT calculations were carried 
out using the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP).
[46,47]  The 
exchange-correlation potential of the electrons was described using the 
generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the Perdew–Burke–
Ernzerhof functional (PBE).
[48]  The projector augmented wave (PAW) 
method was used to describe the electron–ion interaction. [49]  The 
convergence threshold for the self-consistent field calculation was set to 
2 × 10
-6  eV for the energy change. The atomic positions were fully relaxed 
until the Hellmann Feynman force converged to less than 0.02  eV Å -1 . 
The Brillouin zone was sampled with the gamma-centered Monkhorst–
Pack k-point grid: a 4 × 4 × 3 k-point grid for bulk systems and gamma 
point for surface systems.
[50]  Dipole slab corrections were also applied 
to the surface systems. To determine the bulk structure (MA 0.5 FA0.5 P
b0.5 Sn0.5 I3 ), the number of cases for the orientation of organic cations 
(i.e., MA, FA) was investigated. The FA molecules were substituted 
with the MA molecule sites of the MASn
0.5 Pb0.5 I3  structure used in the 
work of Feng et al., [51]  and the lattice parameters and atomic positions 
were fully relaxed. The optimized lattice parameters of the most stable 
structure were a  = 8.80 Å, b  = 9.36 Å, c  = 12.96 Å, α  = 92°, β  = 89°, and 
γ  = 91°. Subsequently, a flat termination of a symmetric (001) surface 
consisting of five PbSnI
4  layers was constructed. The vacuum slab of 
20 Å was added in the z-direction to eliminate self-interaction of the 
surface slab. The optimized surface slab had an E
g of 1.21  eV, similar 
to the experimental value of 1.25  eV. For investigation of the defect 
structure, three types of point defect (i.e., interstitial, vacancy, and anti-
site defects) were introduced to the top layer of the surface slab, and 
the atomic position was again fully optimized (Figure S19, Supporting 
Information).

RESOLFT nanoscopy with 
photoswitchable organic 
fluorophores
Jiwoong Kwon1,*, Jihee Hwang1,*, Jaewan Park2, Gi Rim Han2, Kyu Young Han3,4 & 
Seong Keun Kim1,2
Far-field optical nanoscopy has been widely used to image small objects with sub-diffraction-limit 
spatial resolution. Particularly, reversible saturable optical fluorescence transition (RESOLFT) 
nanoscopy with photoswitchable fluorescent proteins is a powerful method for super-resolution 
imaging of living cells with low light intensity. Here we demonstrate for the first time the 
implementation of RESOLFT nanoscopy for a biological system using organic fluorophores, which 
are smaller in size and easier to be chemically modified. With a covalently-linked dye pair of Cy3 
and Alexa647 to label subcellular structures in fixed cells and by optimizing the imaging buffer and 
optical parameters, our RESOLFT nanoscopy achieved a spatial resolution of ~74 nm in the focal 
plane. This method provides a powerful alternative for low light intensity RESOLFT nanoscopy, which 
enables biological imaging with small organic probes at nanoscale resolution.
Since 1994, a number of far-field optical microscopy techniques have been proposed to overcome the 
optical diffraction limit 1–3. Although each of these fluorescence nanoscopy (“super-resolution imag-
ing”) techniques uses distinct strategy, all of them share an identical core mechanism, i.e., switching 
between a ‘bright’ (fluorescent, “ON”) state and a ‘dark’ (non-fluorescent, “OFF”) state4. In contrast to 
the single-molecule based localization techniques 5–8, the coordinate-targeted nanoscopy techniques such 
as stimulated emission depletion (STED) or ground state depletion (GSD) microscopy generally use the 
reduction of the effective focal volume. This is done by concentrically overlaying a circular excitation 
beam with a donut-shaped depletion beam, leading to the pre-emptive decay of off-center fluorophores 
to a dark state
9,10. The singlet ground state often acts as the dark state in STED while the first triplet 
excited state plays the same role in GSD.
There is yet another approach, simply called RESOLFT (reversible saturable optical fluorescence tran-
sition), which usually exploits reversibly photoswitchable fluorescent proteins (RSFPs) 11–14. Due to the 
fact that the photoinduced dark states are thermally stable15, RESOLFT nanoscopy requires a much lower 
laser intensity than STED and GSD microscopy. It also leads to a low residual fluorescence level. Because 
RSFPs can be easily expressed in living cells via genetic engineering, RESOLFT nanoscopy has been 
considered as a promising tool for biological applications of super-resolution imaging 16–18. For example, 
thanks to the low operating laser intensity, even a living brain tissue was visualized with nanometric res-
olution for a long observation time with negligible photodamage 19. This feature also allows parallelized 
RESOLFT nanoscopy with > 20,000 doughnut-like intensity minima, which greatly reduces the acquisi-
tion time20. Furthermore, a recently developed RESOLFT technique enables a facile dual-color imaging 
of spectrally undistinguishable fluorescent proteins by using the difference of fluorescent kinetics 21.
